en: The Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, appear in the world solely to reveal to sentient beings the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

Now, is this Buddha-knowledge and vision different from the knowledge and vision of sentient beings, or is it not different? If they were indeed different, then sentient beings would be forever excluded from [attaining Buddhahood].
How could the Buddhas appear in the world without cause? If they are not different, then sentient beings are themselves the Buddha.
If this is so, why borrow the instructions of other Buddhas? Thus, whether they are different or not different, all Buddhas do not appear in the world;

yet, for what reason does a Buddha ultimately appear in the world? It is truly because the Buddha knows and the Buddha sees that everyone inherently possesses [this nature], yet due to deluded thoughts and attachments, they cannot directly accept it as their own.
They mistakenly believe that this is something belonging to the domain of a Buddha. It is not...
Know that this does not depart from the ordinary perception of seeing forms and hearing sounds.

For this reason, the World-Honored One Śākyamuni descended into the mundane world and, for over forty years, skillfully governed and guided beings through expedient means. It was only with this sutra that he finally provided a definitive revelation.
This must await the extinction of inverted conceptions and the sincere self-acceptance [of the truth]; it is in no way different from the school of the Direct Pointing of Bodhidharma.
How easy is it to explain the wondrous scripture of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*?

Although there are various commentaries on this sutra from ancient and modern times, and their literary expressions are resplendent and worth beholding, they for the most part remain mired in the trap and snare [of words].

By excessively exalting the sacred realm, they cause the Tathāgata’s subtle truth to be transformed, instead, into a doctrine of names and forms. Only the words and meaning of our Great Master are shallow in expression yet profound in intent, concise in phrasing...

The principles herein are complete. Shedding all branches and leaves, every word directly reveals the fundamental mind; cutting straight to the source, every sentence dissolves back into one's own nature.
This is by no means comparable to those who count the sands of the Ganges or speak of food without eating it. Consequently, practitioners of that time vied with one another to gain access to it.

Yet, as the woodblocks were stored in the Three Wu regions of Eastern Yue, it was inconvenient for fellow dharma-practitioners to obtain them; furthermore, the carving of the blocks had not yet been completed.

Furthermore, there were errors such as those involving the "Emperor Tiger" (Di-hu). [I], being unworthy, have therefore collated the original scripture and the various texts cited therein two or three times.
I have commissioned the public to re-carve the blocks, so that the wondrous flavor of the clarified butter may be shared equally across the great earth.
If readers can grasp the essential meaning beyond the words, they will not fail the venerable Old Master’s single-minded, compassionate heart.

Preface to the "Meaningful Words" of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, written on the full moon day of the second month of summer in the Gengwu year of the Chongzhen era by the Dharma-heir Minghai, who burns incense and bows in reverence.
Now, as for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, it is the wondrous mind that all Buddhas do not transmit. For this mind is...

Its characteristics leave no sign and no trace; words are insufficient to convey it, and discourse is insufficient to discern it. Therefore it is said: "This Dharma has the characteristic of quiescence;

it cannot be proclaimed through speech. Since neither words nor writing can fully exhaust its essential meaning, the metaphor of the lotus is employed to direct the intention beyond the literal expression, so that one may realize it through silent cognition and penetrate it with the mind. Now, as for the significance of the lotus, it is square—*fang*.

The flower having already borne fruit illustrates that the three periods of time do not shift. Its constant purity while dwelling in defilement illustrates the lack of interval between the holy and the ordinary.
Its manifestation without fixed direction illustrates the equality of all sentient beings. A single cluster with many seeds illustrates the cohabitation of the ten realms.

The lotus is but one kind, yet it appears in three states according to its environment: when in the water it is called *fúqú*; when emerging from the water it is called *hàn-dàn*; and when fully blossomed it is called... [the text ends here].
The lotus flower is used as a metaphor for my mind, and it possesses three meanings: when it is in its causal state (*garbha*), it is called "true nature" (*tathatā*);

when it arises, it is called "illusory mind"; and when it is fully manifested, it is called "wondrous wisdom. Therefore, there is a profound reason why I do not employ the metaphor of various other flowers, but instead use the lotus alone.

Furthermore, among ordinary flowers, some blossom first and then bear fruit, while others produce fruit first and then blossom; some are even hollow blossoms without substance. [The lotus, however, is distinct.]

It truly bears fruit, or perhaps many flowers produce a single seed; yet this is not like other flowers where the blossoms open and the lotus appears, or the flowers fall and the lotus is formed, as if there were no distinction between priority and sequence.
Flowers must have fruit, and fruit must have its core; there is no error of empty blossoms that do not result in fruit.
Now, "lotus" (lián) means "continuity" (lián); it is a continuous chain that never breaks, existing everywhere—whether in water, fire, or wood.

Whether it be on stone, on the ground, or in the air, these manifestations accord with what the mind perceives, regardless of the location or direction. For example, when King Gong donated his residence to build a temple, lotuses grew upon the mulberry trees;
when a bhikṣu was practicing the Way in a remote mountain, lotuses appeared within the rocks; due to the karmic retribution from Jotika’s past lives, lotuses blossomed within a fire;
and because a lay devotee recited the Buddha’s name with sincere devotion, lotuses sprang forth from the steps of his courtyard.
Such various examples could not be fully enumerated; they may be inferred by the mind.

Furthermore, the lotus emerging from water is natural, serving as a metaphor for a śramaṇa who, relying on the True Dharma, practices and attains the fruit. A lotus within wood, stone, or fire is not its proper place;
this serves as a metaphor for those of heterodox paths who, relying on false and external ways, practice and yet attain the fruit. Relying on the True...
Those who attain the fruit through the Dharma are, for example, the twelve hundred śrāvakas such as Śāriputra.
Those who attain the fruit by practicing heterodox paths are, for example, Devadatta and King Subhūṣita.

Since the attainment of the fruit does not distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox, is it not like the lotus flower, which does not distinguish between purity and impurity? I maintain that this wondrous Dharma is itself...
The realm of the mind’s constant manifestation cannot be exhausted by words nor known by ordinary consciousness.

The Tathāgata pointed to the lotus flower that is commonly seen as a metaphor for the self-mind that is difficult to perceive, thereby enabling one to grasp it beyond the reach of language. I know that the lotus as a metaphor is truly vast!
As for its other wondrous meanings, they shall be seen in the relevant chapters. I am ashamed that my days of study have been few and my learning and experience remain incomplete.

I have extensively studied the commentaries of several masters, exhausting my efforts for many years. I have come to realize that there exists within them a subtle profundity that the ancients themselves did not fully express.

Undaunted by my own recklessness, I have composed these words of interpretation; though I may be fabricating false views and devising a separate mechanism, my heart’s intent is to praise the Mahāyāna, even if I am willing to bear the error of slandering the Dharma.
It is not necessarily the case that the Tathāgata’s emissary would act in such a manner. I.
The Dharma Master Ju falsely claims to have followed [the master] later, stating:
"At that time, in the forty-second year of the Great Ming Wanli era, the year being Jiayin, at the Ancient Yunmen Xiansheng Temple in Kuaiji."
The Meaningful Words of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* composed by Chan Master Zhanran Cheng of Yunmen. Recorded by Zhanran Cheng, the Abbot.
Revised by Minghai, a disciple of Dongchu.
"The Wondrous Dharma" (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*) is simply another name for one's own mind. "Lotus" (*puṇḍarīka*) is a skillful metaphor for this wondrous Dharma.

Indeed, the wondrous nature of the mind-dharma undergoes a thousand transformations and ten thousand changes beyond what can be fully described; it is not that it cannot be described, but rather that words are insufficient to express it.

To exhaust its profound mysteries, it employs the metaphor of the lotus flower; thus, they resemble one another. This enables people to clarify the mind through material objects and to realize the essential meaning beyond words.
Indeed, this involves setting aside phenomena to grasp principles, departing from defilement to seek purity, severing delusion to realize the truth.
Avoiding clamor and seeking tranquility— through various causes and conditions such as these, which were recorded in the teachings of the Three Vehicles (Triyāna) spoken by the Tathāgata in the past,
those of the Three Vehicles failed to recognize that these were provisional and not ultimate, and thus falsely gave rise to joy and aversion.
Out of compassion for such people, the Tathāgata, after forty years, preached this wondrous Dharma of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna), so that they might know that even within defilement...
"Purity does not exist apart from the defilements. It is like the lotus: its place of origin is the low-lying, damp mud; this is its natural state.

High ground or dry land is not suitable for it. This serves as a metaphor for my mind, which does not abandon the myriad dharmas and thereby accomplishes the roots of goodness of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
If one seeks self-comfort by departing from these dharmas, one falls into the way of the Śrāvakas, which the Buddha does not permit."
One must say: "Only after practicing all the immeasurable Dharma-methods of the Buddhas with courageous diligence will one then accomplish the profound and unprecedented Dharma.
Kāśyapa said: "If one does not take delight in purifying the Buddha-fields and bringing sentient beings to maturity?"
This is the lotus of dry land. Those who have fully practiced the Way and the Dharma are the lotuses from the mud. As the subsequent text says: "This Dharma cannot be shown;
words and signs are quiescent," meaning that the mind cannot be sought through signs. "Cease, cease! There is no need to speak;
my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive," meaning that the mind cannot be conceived through thought. To exhaust all thoughts in an attempt to fathom it—
As for "measurement," that which cannot fathom the Buddha’s wisdom is such that the mind cannot measure it. The principle of one's own mind is subtle and wondrous in this way;

how else could it be clarified than by relying on metaphors? From this, one should know that the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* (The Lotus of the Wondrous Dharma) is a metaphorical representation of the dharma of one's own mind.
"Sūtra" means "path"; it is the path for reaching the wondrous realm of one's own mind. [Old...]
The commentators value only the literary style and are lost in its great principles. I, however, point directly to the human mind and show the shortcut.
If one can grasp the meaning beyond words and speak of one’s own mind, it is utterly unobtainable;

where else, then, could there be a "Wonderful Dharma Lotus"? When asked, the ancients said: "The true mark is the wonderful dharma, skillfully likened to the lotus. You say that the wonderful dharma is oneself—[is this not so?]
How could it not be contradictory to give the mind a different name? Answer: The true reality (*dharmatā*) of one’s own mind is fundamentally not two distinct things.
However, in order to guide sentient beings according to their capacities and provide them with benefit, it is necessary to distinguish them.

If one speaks only of "true reality," there is still fear that students will become stuck in names and concepts, imagining there is a separate dharma, exalting the state of the sages while seeking it falsely outside the mind. Therefore, I simply say "one's own mind" to cause them to turn the light back upon themselves.
Illumination. To know that this is inherently present is to bring rest to the mind of seeking; this resting is itself bodhi, the ultimate destination, which does not contradict the principle.
Preface Chapter.

The "Preface" (xu) means the thread (xu) and the core (zong). By pulling the collar and lifting the main framework, it clarifies the great purport of this single scripture. "Buddha" (*buddha*) is none other than the true mind.
"Rājagṛha City" is the physical body composed of the four great elements. "Gṛdhrakūṭa Mountain" is the union of form and mind.
In the Sanskrit language, *Gṛdhrakūṭa* is translated here as "Spiritual Vulture Peak. Ancient sages referred to the union of form and mind as the "Spiritual Terrace" (*lingtai*). This is...

This is its meaning. It is that the eternally abiding true mind takes form and mind (*rūpa-citta*) as its dwelling place, and form and mind, in turn, take the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) as their locus of dwelling.
The intent is to say: "I have heard that such a Buddha dwells within the interval between the four great elements, form, and mind;
it is not to be sought from without. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* asks: "When one is deluded, this becomes the mind; one is certainly confused by taking form to be [the self]."
Within the body, one does not realize that from the physical form outward, including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth, all are things within the wondrously luminous true mind.
To now say that the true mind is merely lodged between the physical and the mental is identical to the error they themselves have refuted.
How is this clarified? Answer: Your citation of the scripture is incomplete, which is why you remain confused. That text states:
"To take the state of turbid agitation as the nature of the mind" refers clearly to the deluded mind of incessant arising and ceasing, not the true mind that is neither born nor extinguished.
Indeed, the eternally abiding true mind is neither identical to the physical body, nor is it separate from the physical body.
It is neither internal nor external; it is neither not-internal-and-not-external. It is neither empty nor existent, yet it does not destroy emptiness or existence.

It is free from all marks and is identical with all phenomena (*dharmas*). It transcends the path of speech and thought; where the movements of the mind cease, it is truly a realm of self-realization, not something that can be reached through verbal discourse.
Question: If it is indeed as you have said, then after the four great elements have disintegrated, what of the true mind?
In what sense? The answer is: "Two mouths and one tongueless. The term *bhikṣu* (monk) is used in reference to the cause, while *arhat* (worthy one) is used in reference to the fruit.
Each of these, cause and fruit, possesses three meanings. Regarding the three meanings within the cause: destroying evil, terrifying Māra, and the mendicant (*bhikṣu*).
Regarding the three aspects of the fruit: "slaying the thief" means that one does not give rise [to further existence] and is worthy of offerings, for there are no longer any afflictions;

this is the meaning of "slaying the thief. "Not giving rise [to further existence]" means that all fetters of existence are exhausted and the mind attains mastery; this is the meaning of "not giving rise. "Being worthy of offerings" means that all outflows are already exhausted and one has attained one's own benefit;

this is the meaning of "worthy of offerings. Among the enumeration of names, the term "śrāvaka" (disciple) is placed first because they are the primary audience (*yathābhavya*) for this sutra. If one relies upon...

In the general course of the Dharma-gates, all these great bhikṣus are the Buddha’s constant retinue. When traced back to their ultimate source, each and every one is nothing other than one's own mind.
Thus, the Great Master Tiantai said: "The Buddha is the sovereign of the mind; the disciples are the mental factors (*caitta*). Furthermore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* states:

"The assembly of disciples are the various afflictions, transformed according to the will. The commentary on the *Vimalakīrti* cites the *Abhidharma* [Jñānaprasthāna-śāstra], fascicle ten: [text continues].
The enumeration of mental factors (*caitasika-dharma*) clearly elucidates the meaning of the Buddha’s disciples. As the text is extensive, it is difficult to record it in full. The verse says:
Perception, desire, contact, wisdom, Mindfulness, volition, and liberation; Attention toward an object, And concentration through feeling— These are the universal mental factors (*mahābhūmika*).
The enumerated factors assist the mind-king In giving rise to all mental states, Just as a kingdom has ten ministers to provide assistance.
There is one master who presides over each individual matter, and ten disciples who assist the one-minded teacher, each also propagating a single dharma-gate.
Although each presides over one gate, how could they ever not be endowed with the ten virtues? Among the ten mental factors (*caitasika*), whenever one arises, all ten arise accordingly.
Although a specific factor is used for its particular name, in reality, all ten factors are present. Next, the eighty thousand bodhisattvas are listed...
“Sā. Those headed by Mañjuśrī and Avalokiteśvara represent the heart-king within the bonds of saṃsāra, which manifests as the eighty thousand practices of affliction;
yet when it transcends the world, it becomes the eighty thousand gates of the sublime Dharma. Although there are eighty thousand gates, they are governed by wisdom and compassion;
therefore, Mañjuśrī is placed first and Avalokiteśvara second. Once wisdom and compassion are fully possessed, one attains great power; thus, [the next is] followed by Mahāsthāmaprāpta.
Possessing great power and great influence, one is able to advance directly without retreat amidst both adverse and favorable conditions;
therefore, this is followed by Constant Diligence (*nityavīrya*). Through diligence, practice and maintenance are uninterrupted; therefore, this is followed by Non-Cessation (*anirāmiṣa*).

By practicing constantly without ceasing, one is able to produce the Jewel of the Dharma, which is inexhaustible according to its application; therefore, this is followed by Treasure-Palmed (*ratnapāṇi*). [The Jewel of] the Dharma...

Once these are complete, one can respond to illnesses by administering the appropriate medicine, ensuring that no treatment fails to take effect; therefore, this is followed by the Medicine King (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*).

Giving jewels provides sustenance for the body, while giving medicine provides sustenance for the mind. When both wealth and Dharma are given equally, both body and mind are benefited; thus, this is called "courage. Therefore, this is followed by Courageous Giving (*Vīradatta*).
By practicing *dāna* with such vigor, one can transform the fever of the afflictions of stinginess and greed, and immediately attain purity.
It is cool; therefore, it is followed by the Jewel Moon (*ratnacandra*). The Jewel Moon symbolizes wisdom (*jñāna*).

Possessing wisdom, one is able to shatter the darkness of ignorance and achieve great radiance; therefore, it is followed by the Moonlight (*candraprabha*). Once ignorance is shattered, the light of wisdom is revealed alone;
therefore, it is followed by the Full Moon (*pūrṇacandra*). When wisdom is fulfilled, one is able to shoulder the Great Dharma; therefore, it is followed by the Great...
As for power: once power is sufficient, one is able to bear all things simultaneously; therefore, it is followed by "Immeasurable Power.
Once both benefits for self and others are complete, one is able to transcend worldly toil; therefore, it is followed by "Transcending the Three Realms.
Although one transcends the realm of dust, one does not abandon sentient beings but constantly protects them; therefore, it is followed by Bhadrapāla. Such protection is earnest and urgent.
Diligent and tireless, like a mother protecting her child, he is followed by Maitreya, whose compassion flourishes in this world so that one may obtain the treasury of the Great Dharma.
Once the Great Dharma is fully realized, one can become a leader for the multitude, drawing them out from the path of delusion;
thus he is followed by the Teacher. In this manner, these eighty thousand bodhisattvas each [manifest] the virtues of their own minds.
The primary gate is the one that assists the sovereign mind-king; it is likewise not something existing outside the mind.

The subsequent listing of the eight classes of celestial and human beings seated together to hear the Dharma perfectly unifies the distinctions between phenomena and principle, all of which are manifestations of one's own mind.

This first reveals the assembly where the holy and the ordinary dwell in one place; next, it radiates the light of the single boundary between cause and effect; finally, it expounds the One Vehicle of phenomena and principle.
The Dharma reveals its layers upon layers, causing people to believe with single-minded devotion; how solemn it is!
That people cannot directly grasp the subtle intent and instead compete merely over the forms of words is truly lamentable.

Since the *Sūtra of Immeasurable Meanings* was taught to the various bodhisattvas, its momentum could not have been exhausted in a single day; why then, at the moment the assembly gathered, did you say that the preaching of the sūtra was already finished?

This concludes [the section]. Herein there are two meanings. First, by means of the Samādhi of the Boundary of Moments (*kṣaṇāntika-samādhi*), one fuses [time] such that no nature of the three periods can be apprehended.
Thus, the subsequent passage states: "Contemplating that which is remote as if it were this very day; even kalpas as numerous as motes of dust do not differ from this day.
It is thus clear that within a single instant, he expounds immeasurable meanings. Second, at this time, he precisely intends to harmonize the provisional [teachings].
"Returning to the reality" refers to that which was taught during the preceding forty years as the "Infinite Meanings.

At the beginning, one proceeds from the single Dharma of ultimate reality to provide teachings on infinite meanings; thus it is said: "Within the path of the One Vehicle, he teaches three according to what is appropriate.
In the end, he gathers back the infinite meanings and returns to the single reality; therefore, he enters the Samādhi of Infinite Meanings, for this samādhi is not something expressed by words.
This is the point of convergence. The faculties of the various devas are sharp; upon seeing him enter meditative concentration for the first time, they immediately scatter flowers and offer praise.

The bhikṣus in the assembly, however, were divided between doubt and faith. Therefore, the World-Honored One again emitted light from between his eyebrows, for there was a specific intent behind this.
It is because he formerly emerged from the single mind through immeasurable gates of meaning, and now gathers those immeasurable meanings back into the source.
With a single mind: those of superior capacity realize it perfectly all at once, while those of middling and inferior capacity still remain stuck in a sequence of before and after.
Thus, within a single ray of light, the infinite distinctions of the Dharma-realm are perfectly manifested. Now, a single ray of light is not different [from others], yet the Dharma-realm is not one.

Difference is not different from identity; it is difference because of identity. Identity is not identical to difference; it is identity because of difference. Identity and difference are simultaneous, neither preceding nor following.
They are infinitely layered and mutually interwoven, such that they cannot be known by wisdom nor cognized by consciousness.
This is truly the realm of wondrous awakening—how could it ever be reached through words? Light radiates from between his eyebrows.
This is because it is not a place of movement. While all six sense organs have their functions, the eyebrows alone appear to have none;
yet, although they are said to be "useless," this does not obstruct their constant, blazing activity. Therefore, light is emitted from them.
That it emerges from between the two eyebrows, being neither left nor right, reveals the subtlety of the mind-dharma; being neither existent nor non-existent, it is the transcendent Middle Way.

Just as a lotus flower is neither defiled nor pure, yet is not obstructed by defilement or purity—the six realms of ordinary beings being defiled and the four classes of noble ones being pure—all are fully manifested within a single ray of light.
This reveals the principle that all phenomena are mind-only, wherein defilement and purity are harmoniously integrated.
The light shines upon eighteen thousand worlds in the eastern direction, penetrating from the highest to the lowest, reaching everywhere without exception.
The East is the head of all movement; it symbolizes that within the deluded minds of all ordinary beings, this Dharma is inherently present.

Beginning with the fourfold assembly’s initial aspiration, proceeding through the Bodhisattvas’ cultivation of the path, and culminating in the Buddhas’ attainment of perfect enlightenment, the turning of the Wheel of Dharma, and their entry into Parinirvāṇa followed by the construction of stupas and offerings—these matters must span across kalpas and cannot be accomplished in a single moment or a single day.

They are fully manifested within the light; in a single kṣaṇa, the nature of the three periods of time is emptiness. The four classes of noble ones and the six realms of ordinary beings are all simultaneously manifested within this single light;
the ten directions are not separated. Since the ten directions are not separated, why should one abandon the defiled for the pure?

Since the nature of the three periods of time is emptiness, why should one fear death or rejoice in birth? Although the underlying intent is thus profound and subtle, one must know that there is still a direction to follow.
"The ultimate point lies herein. What is this ultimate point? It is simply this: when the Buddha emits light, one perceives all these various distinctions;
yet before the light was emitted, what did one perceive? As the text below states: "This Dharma cannot be shown."
When it is said that both the characteristics of speech and the characteristics of radiance are quiescent, then both the radiance and the speech are prohibited.

Is this not the Buddha’s true intention, that he does not reside in emitting light or in verbal expression? One should know that when he neither emits light nor preaches the Dharma, there is directly beneath one no place for the mind to function.
Therefore it is said: "The light does not illuminate objects, and objects do not exist; when both light and object are forgotten, what else is there?"
Things. Here, one goes forth; there, one returns. Only then does one see that the assembly on Vulture Peak remains solemnly as it was, undispersed. An ancient worthy said:

"If one discusses this matter, those of the Two Vehicles lose heart, and those of the Ten Stages are struck with terror. Even for a Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment, there still remains a fraction of ignorance;
their vision of the nature is like the moon reflected in a net. Now, Maitreya’s rank is that of Equal Enlightenment, yet he remains bewildered regarding this.
In questioning these doubts, one verifies that the words of the ancients were not uttered in vain. Someone may ask:
"If it is claimed that Maitreya was actually harboring self-doubt, does this not incur the fault of slandering a sage? Why is this so?

In the 'Ten Samādhis' chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when Samantabhadra expounds the ten great samādhis, this very meaning is fully revealed. How could he have been unaware of it until forty years later? Its...

To ask for the resolution of doubts is merely to demonstrate the provisional (*upāya*). One must realize, however, that the Dharma-gate is subtle and profound; the provisional and the real (*tattva*) are never fixed as one or the other.

If it were definitively a demonstration of the provisional, then there would be no distinction between the stages of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and Wondrous Enlightenment (*vimala-bodhi*).

Furthermore, the Sūtra clearly states that [the Buddha] wished to resolve his own doubts and observed the minds of the assembly—how could this be a mere one-sided demonstration of the provisional? Zao Bo said: "Equal Enlightenment..."
Looking toward the wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), there still remain one hindrance and two delusions; how could these be anything other than ignorance (*avidyā*)?

Within a single ray of light, Maitreya described what he saw in great abundance, which cannot be fully enumerated and can only be briefly explained. The text is divided into four sections: first, an account of the auspicious signs he beheld;
second, an account of the light illuminating the various lands; third, an account of the retributions received by the six realms of existence; and fourth...
This section recounts how the four sages received benefits; it merely outlines the general points here, while the subsequent chapters will provide detailed explanations of their meaning.

Within this general introduction, both ordinary beings and sages are listed together; however, in the detailed expositions that follow, only the characteristics of the Bodhisattva’s practice are described, and the six realms of existence are not mentioned.

This is because they are not essential to the core of progressive cultivation, and thus are not explained in full detail. Such [beings] as have seen or heard [this teaching], numbering in the billions...
"Affairs" refers to the narration of their vastness. "Gathering mindfulness in mountain forests for hundreds of millions of years" refers to the narration of their duration.

The underlying meaning is that a space as small as a single hair-tip should not be able to contain such a multitude of affairs, and a moment as brief as a single thought should not be able to pass through such a long period of time.
These words are extensive and profound, yet their intent is subtly revealed; it is certainly not [the case that they are]... [incoherent].
He asked again, saying: "World-Honored One, for what reason do you emit this radiance? He further asked: "For what benefit do you manifest this radiance? Again he said:
"The Buddha emits a single ray of light," and again: "You emit a single pure light. In each instance, he questioned specifically regarding the light, as if he did not understand.
In the "Entry into the Dharma Realm" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, when Sudhana enters Maitreya’s tower, he sees...

Within those pavilions, they were adorned with various jewels. In some, he saw Maitreya from his initial generation of the bodhicitta, through his cultivation of the bodhisattva practices, up to his subduing of Māra, his attainment of the Way, his preaching of the Dharma, his entry into nirvana, and the distribution of his relics.
Within each and every pavilion, Sudhana saw all such things, as well as other immeasurable realms of sovereign mastery. Compared to the space between his eyebrows—
The radiance contains a multitude of qualities; what is the distinction between them?
It is truly regrettable that one does not inquire into the clarity of why Maitreya manifests in this way.

Presumably, by the power of samādhi, Maitreya has manifested for Sudhana the realm realized within his own nature, enabling him to see it and thereby providing the benefit of spiritual progress. Now, seeing the Tathāgata suddenly...
Nevertheless, seeing that light was emitted, he knew it could not be without a cause; thus, harboring doubt, he asked a question. Such is the nature of the Dharma.
This matter truly does not belong to the realm reached through the cultivation of supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Previously, Maitreya had raised two doubts:

first, the doubt that the distinctions between the ten realms appear together within a single ray of light; second, the doubt concerning how sentient beings, who initially remain submerged in stagnation, ultimately...
From the time of the Buddhas' parinirvāṇa until now, the events span more than a single kalpa. For what reason, then, do they all assemble together within a single kṣaṇa?
Thus, Mañjuśrī cites the past as his answer, directly revealing the fundamental mind: that the present and the ancient are not different. "Kalpa" (劫) means time or stagnation.
"Inconceivable asaṃkhyeya of the past" refers to that which transcends the reach of thought and speech, remaining unconfined by temporal kalpas. Three... [text ends]

The nature of the world is empty. As for the "Sun, Moon, and Lamp Radiance": the sun can illuminate the day, the moon can illuminate the night, and the lamp illuminates places where both do not reach;

this serves to symbolize the wisdom of perfect luminosity (*paripūrṇa-prabhāsvara-jñāna*). Sentient beings are obscured by this perfect luminosity and remain stuck within the three periods of time, suffering in vain through the cycle of saṃsāra.
The sages’ threefold wisdom illuminates everything perfectly, never subject to coming or going. Thus, one should know that this Buddha is...

The "perfectly luminous" refers to one's own mind. That the twenty thousand Buddhas all share the same name signifies that those of the Two Vehicles possess the same virtues. Furthermore, regarding their sharing the same nature:

previously it was taught that the Buddha and those of the Two Vehicles are as vastly different as heaven and abyss; why, then, is it now said they share the same virtues? It is because their nature is the same.
Not only do those of the Two Vehicles share the same virtues and the same nature, but there is not a single ordinary person who has not yet left the household life who does not likewise [share them].
All are the same. Therefore it is said: "When the final Buddha was still a layman, he had eight princes. Now, there are three kinds of 'homes' from which one departs:
first, the home of ignorance; second, the home of the triple world; and third, the home of worldly convention. Buddhas and Bodhisattvas depart from the home of ignorance.

The followers of the Two Vehicles have departed from the house of the triple world, whereas only ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) do not depart from the house of the mundane; therefore, they are called "ultimate Buddhas.

The followers of the Two Vehicles have already destroyed the six consciousnesses, so in principle they possess no "sons"; ordinary beings, however, still fully possess their conscious minds, and thus the meaning of "sons" is fulfilled in them.
Although they are not called "ordinary beings," they are called "Buddhas" because the Buddha taught that all sentient beings are future Buddhas; therefore, they are the most [ultimate].
The latter refers to the meaning of the future. The Bodhisattva Wonderful Light (*Prabhāketu*) is the seventh consciousness (*manas*).

"Internally taking the lamp-light as one's teacher" means internally relying on the eighth consciousness, the mind-king (*citta-rāja*). "Externally teaching the eight sons and the seeker of fame" means externally acting as the support for the six and five [consciousnesses] regarding defilement and purity.
The eight sons are the sixth consciousness; therefore, they are all termed "mind" (*manas*). The seeker of fame is the first five consciousnesses.

This consciousness takes only the five objects of the conventional truth as its object; hence it is said: "It frequents the families of the noble. It possesses spontaneous discrimination (*svarasa-vikalpa*) but lacks deliberative discrimination (*abhinirūpaṇā-vikalpa*);
hence it is said: "It is forgetful and not sharp. It takes only the present as its object and does not take the past or future as its object;

hence it is said: "It abandons what has been studied and recited. As for your question regarding why one [consciousness] lasts long while another is brief, and why their meeting is without difference—if one were to depart from...
When the mind understands the Dharma, then the distant and the near appear clearly as they are. If one contemplates directly within the mind, then its nature is empty moment by moment;
how could there be past, present, or future? Therefore it is said: "The Bodhisattva Wondrous Light is none other than my own body; the Bodhisattva Seeking Fame is none other than your own body."
Right now, as I observe my own self, is there such a thing as distance and proximity? Or is there no such thing as distance and proximity?
If one can truly awaken, it is like waking from a dream; since even body, mind, and the world do not exist, how could there be any birth and death to be found?

In the "Expedient Means" chapter, there are two kinds of expedient means. First, because the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) of the wondrous Dharma cannot be demonstrated directly, they can only serve as an aid to its manifestation;

thus it is said: "The Buddhas emit radiance to assist in manifesting the meaning of the true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). This serves to further assist those who perceive these signs to resolve their doubts.
Mañjuśrī skillfully guided and answered from the side; those of sharp faculties had already attained awakening, as described in the preceding chapter.
Second, although the Śrāvakas received the same teaching, their understanding varied; even though they beheld the signs, they did not slander or doubt them, yet they were still not fully clear.
They necessarily required verbal explanation and instruction, for although the Sublime Dharma cannot be proclaimed through words, there is no means of guidance other than words. Therefore...

In this context, the Buddha spoke these words of his own accord without being questioned. These two types [of practice] are collectively termed "skillful means. As for the wondrous principle of the true reality (*dharmatā*), it must be realized by each person for themselves.

Although the Śrāvakas have already entered the nature of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*), they become attached to their meditative absorptions (*samādhi*) and, through indolence and self-indulgence, find no joy in teaching and transforming sentient beings within pure Buddha-lands.
Because there were such Bodhisattvas who differed from them, the World-Honored One recounted this in full.
They practice the immeasurable path-dharmas of all Buddhas with courageous diligence, thereby accomplishing profound and unprecedented dharmas to dispel the indolence of the two vehicles.
There are two kinds of these unprecedented dharmas: the first is called the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The second is "all dharmas. Because the śrāvaka has already realized the true mark (bhūtalakṣaṇa), he says: "I and the bodhisattva have both entered the dharma-nature (dharmatā) together.
However, not knowing that all dharmas are themselves the true mark, he becomes weary of teaching and transforming others, and does not wish to adorn the myriad practices (sarvākāracaryā).
To realize this reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) is possible only for the Greatly Awakened World-Honored One. Because he has perfectly realized this Dharma, it is said:
"Only a Buddha and a Buddha can exhaustively fathom the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena. The principle of true reality transcends the paths of speech and thought;

where the activities of the mind cease, neither sound nor form can demonstrate it. Yet, one merely borrows sound and form as skillful means; thus, all phenomena manifest before one, clearly and vividly.

It is not obscure. The hundred realms and thousand suchnesses are perfectly and fully present. How could there be any principle of abandoning the non-true to grasp the true, or of destroying existence to emerge into emptiness?
The followers of the Two Vehicles do not understand this; they falsely claim to leave birth-and-death and enter nirvana, not knowing that birth-and-death is itself nirvana.
They speak of severing afflictions to realize bodhi, not knowing that afflictions are themselves bodhi. Such an instruction is appropriate.
"It is through non-speaking that there is trust. Because Śāriputra had not yet realized this, he respectfully and earnestly requested three times. The World-Honored One first addressed him, saying:
"Such a wondrous Dharma is spoken by the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, only at rare intervals. This may be called a brief statement with vast meaning.
The words are direct, yet the meaning is complete. According to the literal expression, there are only four characters;

yet according to the underlying principle, they point to that which is perceived within the light—the hundred realms and thousand suchnesses, vividly distinct and utterly beyond the reach of thought, mind, speech, or deliberation.
One must simply exercise wondrous discernment prior to words. Yet this wondrous Dharma was not spoken forty years ago; it was only discussed at the very end. Therefore...

It is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower. Now that I know your faculties have matured, I and all the Buddhas reveal it to you, hoping that sentient beings will awaken and enter through it;
there has never been any difference in this. Furthermore, it is not only we Buddhas who act thus;
even all the Buddhas of the ten directions and the three periods of time speak this with one voice and in unison.

The Dharma is likewise without duality. It is only because I and all Buddhas manifest birth in an evil age, and sentient beings are so afflicted by greed and desire that they are unable to receive this Dharma, that we differentiate and speak of three vehicles within the single Buddha-vehicle.
Although we speak of the three vehicles, our intention lies in the one reality. Those who do not understand this are not my disciples; they are not Arhats, nor are they Pratyekabuddhas.

The Buddha said: "Therefore, those among the fourfold assembly of disciples who cling to arhatship as the ultimate goal and no longer strive to seek this Dharma are all people of overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
Those with overweening pride are not true arhats. Why is this?"
If one has truly attained the path of Arhatship, it is impossible that they would not believe this Dharma.

The general meaning is simply that one must have faith in those Buddhas, that there is no other vehicle, but only the Single Buddha Vehicle. In the verse, the first part describes the reason for withdrawing from one's seat.
Next, the intention behind teaching the gradual approach is clarified. The Tathāgata fully knows that the dispositions and desires of sentient beings differ;
thus, to accommodate their inclinations, he provisionally teaches the ninefold Dharma. Although he teaches the nine divisions, they enter into the One as the foundation. Therefore it is said:

"These ninefold teachings of mine are spoken in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings; they have the entrance into the Mahāyāna as their foundation. Now that their faculties have matured, [the Buddha] speaks directly.
The One Vehicle. Therefore, anyone who hears even a single phrase or a single verse shall all attain Buddhahood. However, my original intention lies in the Great Transformation;
I never intend to transform a single sentient being by means of the Lesser Vehicle. To teach and transform others with the Small Dharma would be to fall into stinginess and greed.
Furthermore, it is not only that my attainment of Buddhahood is thus; even when I was in the causal stage, I made a vow that I too would—
Sentient beings are equally liberated. [The Buddha] previously addressed these difficulties, yet they remained deeply pent up in his heart;

today, having finally spoken of his original intention, he is at last satisfied. Thus it is said: "As I have formerly vowed, that vow is now fulfilled. Nevertheless, although the Way is of a single vehicle (ekayāna),...
The capacity of sentient beings cannot be addressed universally; therefore, he further employs diverse skillful means to assist in manifesting the primary meaning.

Beginning with the six perfections and culminating in a single form or a single fragrance—whether raising the head or lowering it—all enter the Buddha-vehicle. Since every form and every fragrance ultimately returns to the path of the Buddha, why was this not taught in the past?
It is only now that it is taught. This is truly because the Dharma is vast while the capacities of beings are small, rendering them unable to receive and comprehend it. Thus he reflects.
He desired to cease his teaching. The devas entreated him, saying that if he did not speak, he would violate their request;

yet if he were to speak, they feared sentient beings would lack faith and would instead damage their roots of goodness. Faced with these two difficulties, he followed the precedent of all Buddhas and expanded this single Dharma into the Three Vehicles.
Therefore, all Buddhas gave their approval in unison, concluding: "Since you have already understood..."
The Buddha, the Teacher of the World, employed skillful means as appropriate to the occasion; thus, our doubts and regrets have vanished, and our hearts are filled with great joy.
We know for ourselves that we shall become Buddhas. Yet, when we contemplate the words of our Original Teacher, how earnest and repeated they were!
We were unable to gain awakening through them, willingly remaining inferior ordinary beings and failing our compassionate grace no small amount.
In the Parable Chapter, Śāriputra, having heard the Buddha’s revelation and awakened to the entry into the One Vehicle, repented of his past errors.

He thus recounted how he had previously heard that bodhisattvas were granted the prediction of attaining Buddhahood, while we ourselves were not included in this matter; yet he constantly reflected that he and the bodhisattvas were equally entered into the dharma-nature.
"How is it that the Tathāgata alone delivers us by means of the Small Vehicle? Could there possibly be partiality in the Buddha's mind?
Only now do we realize that this is not the fault of the World-Honored One, but rather our own failure to understand his teaching according to what is appropriate.

It was our own error to accept, contemplate, and seek realization upon merely encountering [the teaching]. Had we waited for the World-Honored One to explain the reasons for his teaching according to what is appropriate..."
"For those who seek to achieve *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, they must necessarily attain liberation through the Mahāyāna. The World-Honored One confirmed this, saying: "It was not that I withheld it;
rather, those bodhisattvas had already matured their roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*), and upon hearing it, they immediately believed and accepted it.
You have not yet reached such a level, and it would be difficult for you to gain faith; therefore, I did not speak of it immediately. However, today you have attained awakening."
Nor was it an easy matter. In the past, I constantly taught and transformed you in the presence of twenty-two thousand *koṭis* of Buddhas.

Although you have entirely forgotten this, I know that because of the power of your hearing-impressions (*śrutavāsanā*), your roots of goodness have matured; therefore, I preach this sutra for you to lead you into the Buddha-way.
You should also rejoice in this yourself, which is why I immediately grant you this prediction. As for the Buddha named Flower-Light (*Puṣyarāja*), "Flower" symbolizes his causal practice.
Śāriputra takes wisdom as his cause. Wisdom can destroy darkness, just as a flower possesses radiance. By means of the wisdom of the Middle Way, he eliminates the defilements of the two extremes;
therefore, the land is named "Free from Defilement" (Vimalā). By means of the wisdom of equality, he severs the delusions of self and others;

therefore, that realm is level and upright. Because it is free from defilement, it is pure and adorned; because delusions are eliminated, it is peaceful, secure, and prosperous. Delusions severed, defilements [are removed].
It is appropriate that the ground be like lapis lazuli. That Buddha also taught by means of the Three Vehicles for two reasons:

first, because his wisdom was thoroughly penetrating, allowing both the provisional and the ultimate to proceed together; second, because during his causal stage he had his eyes begged for by a brahmin, and thus he knew that the bodhisattva practices cannot be performed all at once.
Therefore, he established vows and spoke in this manner. Whether one fails or does not fail, whether one attains [the goal] or not—[it is as stated].
"It is not so; these are all but reflections of one's own mind. What could they possibly have to do with the Buddha? How profound was Śāriputra’s instruction to me!
Consequently, when the fourfold assembly and the devas heard of his prediction, they all abandoned their former habits and realized for themselves that they would become Buddhas.
Thus, each of them removed their upper robes to offer as an act of worship to the Buddha. Having himself attained awakening, Śāriputra felt compassion for his fellow practitioners."

Again, he addressed the World-Honored One: "Taking the three realms as one's home and pointing to the burning house as one's dwelling, you rely on external objects to instruct and awaken those who have not yet realized the truth;

therefore, this is called 'Parable. The kingdom, the capital, and the villages collectively symbolize the four lands (*catur-bhūmi*). The borders and the sun-kingdom symbolize the Land of Real Reward (*niṣyanda-bhūmi*).

The ministers and officials are called the 'capital,' symbolizing the Land of Expedient Means (*upāya-bhūmi*). The village is a place where human settlements gather, symbolizing the Land of Sentient Beings (*sattva-bhūmi*)."

This serves as a metaphor for the Land of Common Abode (*sahā-loka-dhātu*). The Land of Quiescent Light (*prabhāsvara-loka*) is the essential nature of these three lands; therefore, it is not illustrated separately.

"Elder" (*sthavira*) is a title denoting one whose years and virtue are both flourishing, which is an analogy for the World-Honored One’s four wisdoms being perfectly luminous and his three virtues being fully endowed.
"Immeasurable wealth" is an analogy for the Buddha possessing immeasurable dharma-wealth of merit. The fields can sustain one's life, and the house can provide shelter for the body. By means of...
Samādhi and prajñā are likened to [the master], while skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) are likened to servants. Taking the entire *dharmadhātu* as the household, it is therefore called "vast.
Because there is only the single Buddha-vehicle (*ekabuddhayāna*), it is said that there is "only one gate. Regarding the "many multitudes of people":

because the gate is one while the multitude is many, they cannot be transformed simultaneously, which causes the Dharma to become corrupted and degenerate, leading them to be consumed by the fires of the three poisons and the four inversions.
"Being burned" refers to those who have not yet resolved to attain enlightenment; "a hundred or two hundred people" refers to this state.

"Ten or twenty sons" refers to those who have already resolved to attain enlightenment. If one can indeed resolve their mind [on enlightenment], even if they have not yet escaped the three realms, they have already surpassed ordinary people tenfold.
As for the sons being burned by the fire, their suffering is so acute that their minds feel no revulsion or distress.

As for those with the intent to seek liberation, although they are harmed by the three poisons and the four inversions, they still remain attached to birth and death and are unwilling to advance in their practice.
The elder perceives that his son is in difficulty; filled with alarm, he goes to rescue him. Fearing that the son might not believe him, he contemplates a means to deliver him.

If he were to suddenly attempt to pull him out using supernatural powers (*ṛddhi*) or meditative absorption (*samādhi*), it would be like trying to lift [the child] using a garment, a lap, or a table.
And they departed. These sons were foolish and deluded; they were attached to worldly toil and took suffering for pleasure. What benefit would there be in giving [the wealth] to them?
Therefore, I spoke of things that cause fear in order to stir them. Yet, what can be done about these foolish sons who are neither startled nor terrified?
They do not know what constitutes fire; they do not know the three poisons or the four inversions. They do not know what constitutes the house; they do not know the four [noble truths].

This refers to the great five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). "Not knowing what constitutes a loss" means not realizing that at the moment of a single misstep, one falls into the three miserable realms (*tri-durgati*).
The elder takes the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) as his home; the sons take the five aggregates as their dwelling. The Dharma-realm is eternally peaceful.
The five aggregates are perpetually precarious; therefore it is said: "My pure land is not destroyed, yet the multitude perceives it as being consumed by fire.

Since you do not believe this, I shall again examine skillful means and provisionally speak of the three carts, hoping that they will leave the house. Once they have left the house, I bestow great carts equally upon all.
Thus one knows that the burning house is not real, and the site of tranquility is immovable. It was not bestowed by the elder, nor was anything obtained by the sons. Truly...

It is the fundamental existence; it does not come from without. However, in the prose section, there is only an elucidation of the intent to conceal the ultimate reality (*tattva*) and manifest provisional means (*upāya*), specifically the opening of the One into Three.

As for the delusion of the one mind resulting in the three poisons, the four inversions, and the ten fetters, which leads to the transmigration through the three realms and the cycles of ascent and descent, this is detailed in the verse.
For example, "the elder who has a great house" refers to the site of tranquility (*śānta-maṇḍala*) as the home. This...
If this dwelling is inhabited by the master of right wisdom, then all myriad virtues are fully present.

It is what is called the Hall of Compassion, with meditative concentration as its pillars and foundations, wisdom as its beams and rafters, pure precepts as its base steps, tranquility and insight as its walls, skillful means as its plaster, expedient methods as its thatched roof, and the factors of enlightenment as its eaves and brackets.
These are inherently possessed within one's own mind and do not require seeking from elsewhere; therefore it is said: "The hundred thousand dharmas..."
The gate does not depart from the square inch of the heart; the wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all contained within the source of the mind.

If the deluded children of the five aggregates dwell therein, they are unable to inherit the family legacy. This causes the correct to perish and the heterodox to flourish, virtue to vanish and delusion to appear.
Thus, compassion turns into arrogance—hence it is called "perilous and high. Meditative concentration turns into distraction—hence it is called "crumbling and decayed. Wisdom turns...
Because it constitutes wrong view, it is called "slanted. Wisdom takes precepts as its foundation; when the precepts are broken, the foundation collapses and the steps crumble.

Stopping (*śamatha*) is like the inner walls that protect the chamber, while contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) is like the outer wall that shields one from external views. Because stopping and contemplation are not cultivated, they are said to be "ruined and split apart.
Through skillful means, one recognizes the urgency or slackness of these two: sometimes stopping comes first and contemplation later, and sometimes contemplation comes first and stopping later.

Cease. Having already lost the skillful means, one becomes disordered in both relaxation and urgency; hence it is called "falling into chaos. Regarding the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ*), there is a fixed sequence of rules;
having lost that order, it is called "erroneous omission. Having already lost right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), one takes deluded thoughts as the mind, resulting in obstructions and barriers everywhere;
hence it is called "all-pervasive hindrance and contortion. When the mind loses its correctness, all various afflictions (*kleśa*) proliferate.

Thus it is said that they are filled with impurities. Once the three poisons are complete, they are expanded into the ten fetters (*daśa-anuśaya*), which are further divided into the dull and the sharp.

The dull are likened to insects and birds; the sharp are compared to ghosts and spirits. The presence or absence of these delusive fetters distinguishes the higher from the lower realms. In the first stage, the *Pañcagati-saṃkīrṇa-vāsa-bhūmi* (the ground where the five destinies dwell together), all ten fetters are fully present.
Being oppressed by manifold sufferings, beings seek to emerge into the realm of form (*rūpa-dhātu*); therefore, it is called "crouching upon a mound of earth. As for the realm of form...
Dwelling at the summit of desire, it is like an earthen mound; sometimes rising one or two feet above the ground, this refers to the first and second dhyānas.

Disgusted by the coarse defilements of desire and rejoicing in the purity and subtlety of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), one relies on the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to subdue greed, hatred, and delusion, thereby giving rise to the third dhyāna.

Within this state, there are those of sharp and dull faculties: the sharp attain the four fruits [of the path], while the dull flow toward the realm of empty space (*ākāśāyatana*). Hatred has already been subdued, though its subtle forms remain.

Because their habitual tendencies have not yet been severed, it is like smelling the smoke and embers [of a fire]. Those who previously rushed in all four directions out of hunger and urgency now rely on the food of the Dharma and the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*) to peer into the principle of emptiness and advance in the cultivation of the three dhyānas.
Those of sharp faculties attain this and return to the correct path, emerging from the three realms (*tridhātu*).

Those of dull faculties, however, become addicted to emptiness and refuse to let go; they take the medicine and turn it into a disease, giving rise to the four perversions (*viparyāsa*). Therefore, it is said that "the four directions are filled."

They are blocked. Having already lost the four virtues and carrying the seeds of anger and other afflictions, they flow into the formless realm; hence it is said, "They struggle to run out of their burrows.
Although they are born in the formless realm, they cannot escape being harmed by impermanence; hence it is said, "The kumbhāṇḍa demons seize and devour them as they come.

The elder fully understands these many faults and, in his alarm, instructs and admonishes his sons. When the sons do not believe him, he uses the three carts as a skillful means to entice them. And...
Upon emerging from the house, they were all equally granted great chariots. This shows that the distinctions of rank and order are entirely provisional names.
Once one realizes one's own mind, there is no dharma that cannot be attained. If it were not the family inheritance rightfully belonging to us, how could it be called an "equal gift"?
If one can awaken to the fact that the burning house is not real, then the site of tranquil enlightenment is originally one's own hometown.

In the "Chapter on Resolute Belief" (*Adhimukty-adhikāra*), the World-Honored One previously taught that the three realms are replete with manifold sufferings and pointed to that which lies beyond the realms as peace and bliss. This was a skillful means to entice the children within the burning house;
it merely clarifies the intention of teaching one vehicle while manifesting three. Kāśyapa has profoundly understood how the five periods of teaching encompass and transform sentient beings.
This method [teaches that] the afflictions within those realms are originally my family wealth; those who are deluded and frantic in the burning house are all the legitimate sons of the Buddha.
This may be called skillfully understanding how to preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate.

Because of this skillful understanding, one knows for oneself that we are truly the Buddha’s sons, inherently possessing the vast, perfect merit of the *dharmatā*, no different from the various Bodhisattvas. However...

Due to self-delusion, they lack this aspiration; through false imaginings and attachments, they wander in the cycle of saṃsāra. Now that they have encountered the Noble Vehicle, they have still not reached the ultimate goal.
It is just like a destitute son who, lost to his own hometown, flees to another land; though he is near his father, he does not dare to recognize him.
For over fifty years—though the old texts say "wandering through the five realms," I privately maintain this is not so, for among the various heavens...
Not yet having emerged from birth-and-death is also called being adrift; this constitutes the six realms. Why then are they called "five"? One should say "the five aggregates" (*pañca-skandha*).
For those who do not believe this, later one sees the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* which states: "The fifty years are precisely the five aggregates.
Within the five aggregates, a single thought-moment arises and possesses fifty kinds of evil. At that time, one is unaware and rejoices within oneself. How [could this be otherwise]?
To "anticipate the turbid age and aspire to meet the Buddha's intent" means to travel through the four directions; this refers to transmigrating through the four modes of birth.

To "seek food and clothing" refers to relying on and grasping at craving and attachment. To "gradually head toward one’s native land" refers to wearying of suffering and seeking joy by relying upon worldly wisdom.

The period for severing afflictions refers to what is called "relying on the heterodox to manifest the orthodox," as in the case of Kāśyapa and others, who all entered the Buddha-vehicle from among the non-Buddhists.
As for his father previously coming to seek his son and not finding him, this means that within the stage of the *dharmakāya*, he did not perceive the capacity [of the sentient beings].
"He stayed in a city where his family was very wealthy" and so forth is a metaphorical explanation of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*. This refers to the previous encounter with the original source.

"In the country, one practices according to the teachings of others; though one may slightly subdue the afflictions, this is not yet the Buddha-vehicle. Now that you have reached the city where your father dwells, you have already joined the assembly of the Buddhas.
Your father has realized the Dharma-body, while you, my son, still cling to the five aggregates. The separation between the holy and the ordinary constitutes our parting.
Because you stubbornly cling to the five aggregates, you are unable to realize the twofold emptiness of persons and phenomena. These treasures of the Dharma, the family wealth of mine—"
There is no one to whom I can entrust [this teaching], and for this reason I am grieved.

As for the son who arrived at the house and stood by the gate, he was practicing according to the heterodox teachings of external paths, hoping thereby to transcend birth and death. Seeing that his father was wealthy and noble, he wished to depart;
though he had previously attended great assemblies, he still clung to biased views. Having different endowments from the start, he neither saw nor heard this Great Dharma. He was poor...
That "clothing and food are easily obtained in the village" refers to the external teachings, wherein there is cultivation and attainment.

That "the elder, upon seeing his son, recognized him and felt joy in his heart" is like the Universal Radiance Hall, where one contemplates and knows that all sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata, and thus exclaims, "How marvelous!
Because the Buddha commanded the Bodhisattvas to expound the merits of the forty-two stages (*bhūmi*), it is said, "go and seize [him]."

The followers of the Two Vehicles do not believe; thus it is said they "accuse him of resentment. Because they do not believe, they are struck with alarm and fear; because they do not understand, they fall into a swoon.

To cease the Great [Vehicle] and provide the Small [Vehicle] is like spraying cold water on them. He repeatedly dispatches Bodhisattvas to employ the means of "identical activity" (*samānārthatā*) to gather them in, like sending a man with a squinted eye.
When the impoverished son first takes his wages, he is one who cultivates the cause out of a longing for the fruit. The elder sheds his precious, noble robes and puts on tattered, filthy clothes.

"To conceal his body of a thousand *zhang* and manifest a form of sixteen *zhang* means to hide his true nature while appearing in a limited form. To hold a refuse-basket and appear as if he were fearful means to show himself as an ordinary person while practicing the realization of emptiness to sever the fetters.

'By means of skillful means, he was able to approach his son' means that he concealed the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and manifested provisional teachings (*upāya*), preaching the Four Noble Truths so that the capacity of the recipient and the teaching were in harmony.
You should always perform this work and not go elsewhere; I shall bestow [further grace] upon you."
Your "price" is this: advancing in the four foundations of mindfulness, you shall obtain the four right efforts;
having no hesitation regarding whatever utensils, rice, flour, salt, vinegar, or similar items you require, you shall obtain the four bases of power;

furthermore, providing for those who need aged or infirm servants, you shall obtain the five faculties and the five powers; and being free from deception, indolence, anger, resentment, or complaints, [you shall obtain the seven factors of enlightenment].
He has attained the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*). He does not see you at all as possessing these various evils; he has attained the eightfold noble path (*āryāṣṭāṅgamārga*).

Since the thirty-seven factors of awakening (*saptatriṃśadbodhipakṣadharma*) are now complete, they possess the significance of having a son; therefore, he further bestows a name upon you and calls you "son.

Although you rejoice in this encounter, it is a joy in realizing the factors of the path (*mārga-pakṣa*). Yet, you still call yourself a lowly hired laborer, not yet daring to acknowledge [your true status].

They are Bodhisattvas. After this period, those whose mental states are characterized by mutual trust and who enter and exit [the teachings] without difficulty, will not cling when hearing the Small [Vehicle], nor will they slander when hearing the Great [Vehicle].
Regarding the Vaipulya [teachings], they shall determine what is to be accepted or rejected according to their respective capacities.

Within the Prajñā assemblies, they shall instruct and transform the Bodhisattvas; because they act as the Buddha’s representatives in preaching the Dharma, I entrust them with the charge that they must apply themselves with diligent care.
Do not let it be lost or wasted. He took charge of the communal property without any desire to take for himself.

As for his dwelling remaining in its original location, even though he was taught by the Bodhisattva, he considered himself beyond the reach [of such realization] and did not dare to undertake the Great Dharma.

After a short time had passed, when the king, ministers, and others were gathered together and the family estate was entrusted to him, this was precisely the occasion of his receiving the prophecy (*vyākaraṇa*) within this assembly.

The subtle meaning of the *Contemplation Sūtra* is that Kāśyapa and the others were all designated as "blind men," while we ourselves are all merely deluded, frantic sons of poverty acting as hired laborers.
This was originally intended as a skillful means; it directly captures the Buddha’s fundamental intention.

If one could immediately realize where to return, why would the World-Honored One have needed to expend so much mental effort? If this is truly so, then even if they seek the three chariots outside the gate, how can that compare to this?
Sitting securely within the house,
Kāśyapa and the others have already understood the intent behind the Buddha’s teaching according to what is appropriate; therefore, the World-Honored One confirms this for them, meaning:
You know only that the Tathāgata has taught the One Vehicle as the Three Vehicles according to what is appropriate;
you do not know that the Tathāgata can further manifest the One Vehicle as immeasurable vehicles. Such merit is infinite and boundless;
only a Buddha can know it. Even if you were to speak for immeasurable billions of kalpas, you could not exhaust it. Why is this? Because the Buddha is all...
The King of Dharma has profoundly realized both provisional and ultimate wisdom, attaining mastery over all phenomena;

therefore, he further employs the metaphor of medicinal herbs to expand upon this. The superior, middling, and inferior faculties are used to represent the three vehicles (*triyāna*), while the three types of grasses and two types of trees are distinguished as the five natures (*pañcagotra*).
This merely states the general outline; however, if one relies on the teaching delivered in a single voice, each according to their kind shall receive it.
Explanation: There shall be immeasurable vehicles for immeasurable dispositions; therefore, it is likened to the rain of the heavens falling universally upon the great earth.
Among the myriad phenomena, from the vast to the minute, there is none that does not receive benefit. The rain is moistening without intention, and the things receive it without intention.
Being moistened without intention, those above and below cannot be different; receiving without intention, self and other [cannot be distinct].

There is no difference between them. This is because while the rain is always uniform, the objects it encounters are always diverse; thus, the objects receive benefit without being aware of it, and the rain provides moisture without possessing sentience.
To take these insentient clouds and rain as metaphors for the Tathāgata’s numinous wisdom may seem inconsistent;
however, they serve merely to illustrate how the Tathāgata benefits all things with impartiality, rather than to illustrate how the Tathāgata discerns individual capacities to bestow benefit.
It is a thing. If one relies upon its spiritual intelligence, it is said: "The Tathāgata perceives and knows the destination to which all phenomena tend;
he also knows the deep mental activities of all sentient beings, penetrating them without obstruction. It further says: "I am the all-knower, the all-seer," and so on, up to:
"He observes whether the faculties of these sentient beings are sharp or dull, vigorous or indolent."

Without indolence, he preaches the Dharma according to what each being is capable of receiving. Thus we know that the Tathāgata’s numinous wisdom is far removed from the insentience of rain and clouds;
likewise, the wondrous nature of sentient beings differs from the lack of consciousness found in grasses and trees.

For while grasses and trees are insentient objects that, though they receive the moisture, do not themselves know they have benefited, sentient beings hear the Dharma and obtain benefit, thereby advancing.

Their descent and ascent are clearly visible. As Śāriputra said: "Hearing the Buddha’s gentle voice, so deep, far-reaching, subtle, and wondrous, and dwelling securely within true wisdom, I am certain that I shall become a Buddha.
Furthermore, whenever he finished preaching the Dharma, he would invariably conclude by saying:

"When this Dharma was heard, so many persons attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*); so many persons attained the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika-bhūmi*); so many..."
Some people have attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, while others have resolved their minds upon Bodhi; how could they be the same as insentient grasses and trees?
Yet they are still called "insentient" [in comparison]. In immeasurable lands, even the name of this sutra cannot be heard, let alone being seen, received, upheld, read, or recited.
That we, who are but ordinary beings, have been able to hear this sutra and receive, uphold, read, and recite it—[this is truly rare].

One has already far surpassed and excelled the two vehicles. Yet, if one clings to being an ordinary person, does not believe in attaining Buddhahood, and fails to cherish oneself, then one’s understanding of the Way remains obscure across both past and present, and one’s practice is inferior to that of common folk; how could this not be the same as being like grass and trees?

In the "Chapter on Bestowing Prophecies," it is explained that Kāśyapa has realized the truth and will certainly attain Buddhahood; therefore, the Buddha bestows a prophecy upon him. The preceding text states:
"Whether śrāvakas or bodhisattvas, having heard the Dharma I have preached—even so much as a single verse—they shall all undoubtedly become Buddhas. Having heard even one...

If even one who merely recites the verses attains Buddhahood, how much more so for one who fully understands and preaches the Dharma according to what is appropriate—how could such a person not receive a prediction [of enlightenment]?

Thus, since it is already said that he will undoubtedly become a Buddha, why is a prediction necessary? It is because, in order to cause future beings to give rise to longing and aspiration, a prediction must be granted.
Now, as for the conferring of a prediction: it is a record of his causal mind and resultant awakening, which differ from one another by no small interval. Kāśyapa’s...
In the center, he used refined gold to adorn the broken Buddha within the stupa; therefore, he was moved by this to have a body with golden light.
When he emitted light, it eclipsed the light of the sun and moon, just as a mass of ink would; for this reason, he was called Kāśyapa (Drinking Light). The Buddha was thus named "The Radiant One."
This is due to what the mind has evoked. As for the land named "Radiant Virtue" (Guangde), its radiance swallows the sun and moon; this is the virtue of its light.
As for the eon named "Great Adornment" (Dazhuangyan), among all merits, the merit of the Buddha is the greatest. Because he adorned the Buddha with gold, he obtained such a reward as this.

Regarding the statement that "the realm of the land is adorned and free from all impurities and evils": because one has cultivated the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), the mental faculty ceases;
thus, the defilements of greed and anger do not arise, and impurities naturally vanish. When consciousness is empty, discriminative thoughts do not arise; how then could there be high or low?
Since the defiled mind has already ceased, perfect clarity and awareness are attained without depending on mental conceptions. It is only fitting, therefore, that this be the [Pure] Land.
It is like lapis lazuli. Thus, these causes—the mind—and their effects—the awakening—do not transcend one's own self; how could there be an external Buddha to be realized?
Although Kāśyapa has already received his prediction, Maudgalyāyana and the others seem to believe yet do not believe; they wish to grasp that which is difficult to grasp.
Therefore, he spoke in verse to make a formal request: "If you say we have no share, Śāriputra and Kāśyapa were both my fellow practitioners.

If you say we do have a share, yet we have not received it from the Buddha, we can never truly claim it for ourselves. It is like a royal feast that, though present before us, we would not dare to take on our own authority without the King’s command.
For this reason, the World-Honored One, in accordance with the individual dispositions of each, bestowed the transmission upon them.
This is the record. Subhūti was foremost among those who understood emptiness; having realized and entered true emptiness, he did not discard illusory existence.

Therefore, the Buddha named his land *Nāmasaṃjñā* (Name and Appearance). Within true emptiness, all manner of jewels are fully present; therefore, the eon is named *Ratnasaṃbhava* (Possessing Jewels).
Since all dharma-jewels emerge from within true emptiness, the country is named *Ratnasaṃbhava*. Because he understands emptiness, there is no contention; because there is no contention—
The mind is without high or low. Because the mind is without high or low, it causes that land to be level and upright. That the ground is made of lapis lazuli is the essence of emptiness;
that it is adorned with jewel-trees is the function of emptiness. That there are no mounds, pits, sand, or gravel is also the retribution for the absence of contention.
When there is no contention, frivolous proliferation does not arise; therefore, there is no impurity of excrement or urine. Emptiness is the sublime transcendent reality.
Because of these causes, precious flowers are spread upon the ground and the people all dwell within pavilions; this is a sign of breaking through existence to emerge into emptiness.
Since they are free from contention, they are joyfully followed by others; thus, his disciples are immeasurable and the assembly of Bodhisattvas is likewise countless.
Kātyāyana was foremost among those skilled in debate; because in his causal stage he swept the ground and plastered the stūpas, he now reaps the fruit thereof.
