Because he was the cause [of this], he received the title "Jambū-golden Light. Because he used debate to eliminate heterodox views, his land became level and even.
When one perceives such levelness, the Tathāgata’s stage of nature (*tathāgatagarbha*) is pure and clear; thus, he brought about glass as the ground.
Because he adorned the Buddha-dharma with wondrous eloquence, he obtained the adornment of precious trees. When the Buddha-dharma flourishes and excels, then Māra and externalists cannot prevail.

Because he did not encroach [upon others], he was moved to experience the golden-cord boundary-paths; because he expounded the Buddha-dharma, the rain of the True Cause (saddhetu) fell constantly, whereby wondrous flowers covered the ground.
Those who heard the Dharma obtained the True Cause, and thus there were no four evil realms of existence. Maudgalyāyana was foremost in supernatural powers (ṛddhi);
because during his causal stage he had offered precious incense to the Buddha, he was moved to experience being foremost in spiritual feet (pāda). The Buddha’s name was Tāmālapatra.

The sandalwood fragrance is the symbol of supernormal powers (*abhijñā*). These powers transform the multitudes, and there are none who do not rejoice; therefore, the eon is named "Fulfillment of Joy.

When the multitude beholds these supernormal powers, their minds and intentions are filled with delight; therefore, the land is named "Delightful Mind. Because the power of the divine feet dwells in space, the soil of that realm is level and even.
Because supernormal powers are unimpeded and both interior and exterior are luminously pure, the ground is made of crystal. It is adorned with precious trees.
Austere and universally pure, his supernatural powers gather disciples most extensively; thus, gods, humans, bodhisattvas, and śrāvakas are all immeasurable in number.
Contemplating the origins of this: Kāśyapa cultivates the samādhi of cessation; when the mind ceases, one realizes emptiness. Therefore, Subhūti follows him.
Having realized emptiness, one attains unimpeded eloquence. Therefore, Kātyāyanīputra follows him. Eloquence—
When the mind-ground is clarified, one shall attain supernormal powers; therefore, Maudgalyāyana follows next. These are all manifestations of one’s own mind.

For this reason, those who wish to realize their own mind should take the cessation of mental activity as primary. When recording his attainment of Buddhahood, it is invariably stated that he made offerings to so many Buddhas and constructed so many stupas;
this is because the Dharma-body and the Reward-body are not to be conflated. The Dharma-body is realized solely through...

Because they were awakened by causes, Kāśyapa and others attained a single-minded faith in their own minds and were immediately granted predictions of enlightenment; thus, the Reward Body (saṃbhogakāya) was also produced.

Since it is produced by causes, one must cultivate merit and virtue extensively before it can become perfected. Therefore, know that as for the causal mind and the resultant awakening, there are certainly not two separate persons;

yet, regarding the depth or shallowness of their merit and wisdom, it is difficult for them to be of one kind. While those of the three vehicles equally enter the Dharma-nature, how could there be two different minds?
However, the śrāvakas do not find joy in purifying buddha-fields or bringing sentient beings to maturity; thus, a distinction is formed.
It is like an elder who, upon seeing his son, recognizes his fitness and immediately bestows family property upon him;

yet he must wait until that son has accomplished his great aspirations and humbled his former mind before finally entrusting him with the entire estate. Once the son has received this heavy trust, he establishes himself and achieves [his goals] in the interim.
He was known for his integrity and conduct. Once such conduct is perfected, one becomes a leader for future generations;
yet if one is indolent while desiring to attain that rank, it will surely be difficult.
In the "Parable of the City of Illusion" chapter, the illusory city is unreal and the treasure land is not real; this parable is taught to reveal that both are non-existent.

In the preceding chapter, the three vehicles were permitted as one, leading one to suppose that the three are provisional while the one is real. How can it be known that even this one is not real? If the one were truly real, [the teaching would be complete].

What is meant by "equally bestowed"? If it is equally bestowed, who is it that receives it and who does not? This is truly because those of the Three Vehicles stagnate in the Lesser Vehicle and fail to advance;
therefore, a provisional metaphor of a "transformed city" is used. Upon exiting the city, it is simply said that "the place of treasure is near," rather than specifying a particular location.
This is because both the "Three" and the "One" have vanished, pointing back to one's own mind as the ultimate destination. Now, one's own mind has no trace and no form. It is not...
It can be known through wisdom (*jñāna*), but it cannot be cognized by consciousness (*vijñāna*). If this were not a metaphorical entrustment, by what means could it be elucidated?

As for "Greatly Pervasive and Wisely Victorious" (*Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū*): that the Way encompasses all is called "Great"; that virtue reaches everywhere is called "Pervasive"; and that wisdom guides humans and devas is called "Victorious."

All are images of one's own mind. This mind is vast, encompassing all without exterior; it is subtle, penetrating all without interval. Because it has no exterior, it is great; because it has no intervals, it is pervasive.
All phenomena of the mundane and supramundane worlds arise from this; therefore, it is called "supreme wisdom. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says:
"In a single thought-moment, universally observe immeasurable eons; there is no going, no coming, and no abiding. Thus one understands the three...
Worldly affairs transcend all expedient means to achieve the Ten Powers (*daśabala*). To universally observe the immeasurable in a single thought-moment is "Great Pervasion" (*mahāvyāpti*).
To transcend expedient means and achieve the Ten Powers is "Supreme Wisdom. Based on this, how could this not be one's own mind? Zao Bo said:
"The ten ages of past and present, from beginning to end, do not depart from the present moment; the boundless oceans of lands, self and other, are not separated by even a hair’s breadth."
[The Master] said: "To state it plainly, this mind has no time and no place. Since there is no time and no place, nothing but a metaphor can clarify it;
therefore, we borrow 'immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable' (*asaṃkhyeya*) as an analogy. The Sanskrit term *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* translates here as 'incalculable time.
This is not merely a large number of countless things, but rather the 'countlessness of the countless. Fearing that people might not believe this, he further cites..."
Using dust and ink as metaphors—how could these ever be reached by the limits of thought or calculation? If one dissolves them within one’s own mind, they neither go nor come;
they are without time and without place. Because they are without time, I, by the power of the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, perceive that which is remote as if it were this very day.
Because they are without place, the Brahmās of five hundred million lands in each of the ten directions...
"O Celestial King, you hold flowers to offer to the Buddha. Those from the east say they see the Buddha in the west; those from the south say they see the Buddha in the north;
and so on, even those from above say they see the Buddha below. Is this not, in every time and place, the Great Pervasive Penetration?
To see the Buddha wherever one is—how is this not the Supreme Wisdom? To sit at the site of enlightenment for ten kalpas..."
Regarding the non-manifestation of the Buddha-dharma: if one’s own mind abides in the state of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), there is nothing that can be taught as the Dharma;

hence it is said, "The Dharma-Buddha does not preach the Dharma," and again, "This Dharma cannot be shown; words and signs are quiescent. As for the manifestation of the Buddha-dharma after ten minor kalpas have passed:
this is because one has transcended the state of true reality to employ skillful means (*upāya*). Therefore it is said: by...
By the power of skillful means (*upāya*), he preached for the sake of the five bhikṣus. Furthermore, it says:

"Reflecting upon the power of skillful means practiced by the Buddhas of the past, I too, having now attained the Way, should likewise preach the Three Vehicles. Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū represents the single mind; the sixteen princes represent the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*).

The fundamental consciousnesses are only eight, each possessing both the phenomenal (*vastu*) and the principle (*tattva*); when these are expanded, they become sixteen. Although there are ten names [in the text], [the meaning remains as above].

Sixth: Its essence is solely the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*). Because this consciousness contains all seeds of both the mundane and supramundane realms, it is able to bring to fruition all merits of both the mundane and supramundane realms;
therefore, the first is named "Accumulation of Wisdom" (*Jñānasaṃcaya*). The mind is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
Consciousness is that which acts without restraint; thus, at the request of his son, he turned the Wheel of Dharma in three phases and twelve aspects.
This was the opening of the provisional means (*upāya*). Once the provisional means were opened, it was necessary to lead toward the ultimate reality.

Therefore, it is said: "These venerable śrāvakas have all already achieved [their goal]; you should also preach for us the Dharma of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. This, then, is by means of consciousness.
Contemplating the mind is the image of the Buddha preaching the Dharma. That you have attained awakening is the image of the mind transforming consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Internally receiving the Buddha’s teaching and externally transforming your fellow students is the image of the sovereign (*rāja*) transforming his domain. When internal reception is complete, self-benefit is perfected;
when external transformation is achieved, the benefit of others is fulfilled. Since both benefits are sufficient, it is fitting that you shall attain Buddhahood. If you but know this...

When one's own mind is fully endowed [with the nature], one receives illumination within the mind itself and need not seek it externally. Although there is no need for external seeking, this does not preclude differences in the capacity of those faculties—whether sharp or dull.
Those of sharp faculties comprehend before words are even spoken, thereby knowing that they have long since attained Buddhahood;
thus, there are those who achieved realization in the past. Next are those who attain sudden enlightenment in the present moment; hence they are called "present-time Śrāvakas. Following them are...

These [beings] shall attain [realization] in the future; therefore, they are called "disciples of the coming age. What is explained in this chapter is actually initiated by the Introductory Chapter (*Nidāna*).

In that [chapter], Maitreya perceives an auspicious omen and gives rise to doubt, while Mañjuśrī answers by citing ancient precedents. He clarifies that even across distant kalpas, there is no separation from a single thought-moment (*ekakṣaṇa*).

He shows that what is the concern of Bodhisattvas is a source of doubt for Śrāvakas, and that for those like us who have only recently set their minds [on enlightenment], we are utterly without such a share.

He knew for certain that his own roots of goodness could not be compared to even a single speck of dust across kalpas; yet, because he did not know this, he conceived a sense of inferiority and remained stuck at the "transformed city.
The Tathāgata spoke provisionally of the "Jewel Place" to shatter that attachment. Once the transformed city has been left behind, the Jewel Place has no fixed location.
It is simply said that [enlightenment] is near. If one awakens to one's own mind, even Buddhahood cannot be attained; how much less can there be any distinction between Śrāvakas and Bodhisattvas?
— From the "Chapter on the Prophecy for the Five Hundred Disciples."
The preceding chapter used metaphors to clarify that distant causes [lead to Buddhahood]; thus, it is known that all śrāvakas are bodhisattvas. Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra attained awakening through this.
For this reason, the compiler of the sūtra recounts these three matters in succession to reveal his intention.

Having understood the nature of shadows and echoes, his mind became pure and he leaped with joy, praising the Buddha’s rarity. He further thought: "The virtues of the Buddha are immeasurable; our words cannot fully proclaim them. I...
The Buddha fully knows his inner secrets and outer manifestations, as well as the profound depths of his original vows; he shall therefore proclaim them.

Thus the World-Honored One declared that the teachings expounded by the Buddhas of the three periods of time are all supreme, thereby clarifying that he was not a śrāvaka but was in fact a bodhisattva.
Since Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra was thus, we know that when Śāriputra heard he was to become a Buddha, his mind was filled with great alarm and doubt;

and when Kāśyapa described his purification of buddha-fields and his transformation of sentient beings, his heart felt no joy. This is not because they did not all seek to remedy the ailments of those who came after them.
Furthermore, the Śrāvaka and the Bodhisattva possess only two names, yet never two minds. Since there are no two minds, [the distinction is merely nominal].

"How could we two alone not be sons of the Buddha? Since the Śrāvakas were unable to recognize themselves as the Buddha’s legitimate sons, the Bodhisattvas—while concealing their inner [realization] and manifesting outwardly—engaged them through the means of 'harmony' (samānārthatā).

In this context, the detailed account of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra’s accomplishment of vast Buddha-activities truly initiates the principle of 'concealing within and manifesting without. Because of this inner concealment..."
Because his causal practices were profound and far-reaching, the Buddha’s lifespan is immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas.

Because he proclaims the Dharma with the lion’s roar, revealing the outflow-free (anāsrava) state, the Buddha is named Dharmaprabhāsa. Because the benefit of his preaching is vast, he takes as many trichiliocosms as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River to constitute a single buddha-field.
He proclaims and clarifies the True Dharma, causing sentient beings to advance in goodness and retreat from evil.

Because they have perfected the wholesome, they experience the seven precious jewels as the ground. Because evil has been eliminated, they experience a land free of mountains and hills, and even devoid of women, sexual desire, and the like.

As they have abandoned evil and become purely virtuous, humans and devas interact with one another, and they attain great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) identical to the Buddha’s marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).

This resembles the teaching of the Vehicle of Humans and Devas (*manuṣya-deva-yāna*), wherein there are immeasurable nayutas of bodhisattvas. It also resembles the teaching of the Mahāyāna, [wherein] the sound...
That the number heard was incalculable seems to suggest the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), yet it lacks mention of the Pratyekabuddha Vehicle; this is merely due to the brevity of the text.
That these twelve hundred people all desired to receive a prediction of their future enlightenment is like those who, having partaken of the king’s banquet, hope for the king’s decree.

That they share the same name, "Universal Radiance" (Samantaprabhāsa), is because they have equally attained illumination through the Four Noble Truths. The three vehicles alike contemplate the Four Noble Truths, each attaining what is called awakening. This is so.
Knowing the Four Truths as the primary beginning of the Three Vehicles, he first records Dignāga because he was the first to comprehend the Four Truths.
Regarding the Buddha’s allowance of one thousand two hundred [monks], yet the separate mention of five hundred: these five hundred were present in the assembly, while the remainder were outside.

Therefore it is said: "Those who were not present at this assembly, you should proclaim the teaching for them. Previously, Kāśyapa and the others understood the Buddha’s teaching according to his skillful means;

thus they cited the parable of the impoverished son. Just as the precious wealth within the storehouse was originally one's own property, yet because of inferiority and incapacity, he could not immediately recognize it, causing the elder to labor in employing skillful means to entice and guide him through various forms of training over twenty years.

In recent years, I have finally come to understand that [the teaching] should be divided; yet the meaning seems somewhat remote and circuitous. Herein, it is illustrated by the metaphor of the jewel beneath one’s garment:

it was never originally something external, and could have been used at will, yet through self-delusion and turning away from it, one has suffered in vain from poverty. This realization feels even more intimate.

Within the treasury beneath the garment, there seems to be a distinction between superior and inferior. According to the old accounts, when the Buddha was one of the sixteen princes and preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* on their behalf, he planted [seeds].

"Mahāyāna seed. This is the tied jewel. Now I grant you the prediction of enlightenment," and he immediately showed him the jewel. This person merely understands the general outline of the teaching gate, yet does not comprehend his own livelihood.
Formerly, when Nanyue studied under the Sixth Patriarch, the Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from?
He replied, "From Mount Song. The Patriarch asked, "What thing comes in such a manner? Nanyue did not know how to answer. Eight years passed before—

He said to the Patriarch, "I have spoken it. The Patriarch asked, "How did you speak it? He replied, "To describe it as a thing is not to hit the mark. The Patriarch asked, "Is there still cultivation and realization?
He replied, "Cultivation and realization are not non-existent; however, one must not be defiled by them. The Patriarch said, "So it is, so it is.
Bound once and shown once, [Huineng] remained for only eight years. Furthermore, there was the case of being bound and shown simultaneously.
Regarding "demonstrating": it is like when Master Dazhu went to visit Mazu. Mazu asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Yuezhou.
Mazu asked, "What do you intend to seek by coming here? He replied, "I seek the Buddha-dharma. Mazu said, "You fail to look after your own precious treasure."
"What is the point of abandoning your home and wandering away? Huizhu said, "Which of these is my own family treasure?
The Patriarch said, "That which is questioning me right now is your treasure-trove. It is complete in every respect; its use is entirely at your disposal. Why do you seek it elsewhere?"

Zhuzhu grasped its essential meaning; furthermore, there were those who never again became deluded or turned their backs on it, such that it was manifest in daily life, functioning spontaneously and with mastery—just as when Yangshan saw Dongsi.
Dongsi asked him, "Where are you from? Yangshan replied, "I am from Guangnan. Dongsi said:
"I have heard that there is a 'Bright Pearl of the Pacifying Sea' in Guannan. Is this true? Mount said, "It is. The Master asked, "What is this pearl like?
Mount said, "In the dark moon it is hidden; in the bright moon it appears. The Master asked, "Can you bring it here? Mount said, "I can bring it.
The Master asked, "Why then do you not present it to me, the old monk? Mount said, "Yesterday I arrived at Mount Mui, and there too I was asked for this very thing."
The pearl—there was nothing he could say in response, nor any principle he could advance. The Abbot then granted his request.

If this is so, why must one seek far back through kalpas of time, becoming lost and turning one's back on one’s own mind? If one can directly accept it as such, it has been possessed from the very beginning.
If one merely clings to the path of teachings as being definitive, who would not be called lost and turned away?
In the chapter on the bestowal of predictions upon those in training and those beyond training, Ānanda is the younger brother of the Buddha and Rāhula is his son.

That the prediction is bestowed upon those who follow later—proceeding from the outside to the inside, and from the distant to the intimate—is intended to manifest the principle of putting others first and oneself last; it is the ultimate expression of equality. Regarding these two individuals...
The record [of his] kalpa, land, adornments, lifespan, and retinue—all surpassing those of the bodhisattvas—clarifies that his causal roots were profound.
Ānanda and the Buddha both resolved their minds for enlightenment simultaneously; yet he did not seek swift realization, but instead made a firm vow to protect the Dharma.

Rāhula appeared before the Buddha as the eldest son while secretly practicing the holy life (*brahmacarya*). This was intended to reveal the stagnation of the lesser śrāvakas; thus, it was indeed appropriate.

He was recorded as dwelling above the bodhisattvas. That these two received their predictions simultaneously, and that their eons, lands, and lifespans were all equal, serves to manifest that their understanding and practice were simultaneous.
Ānanda upholds the Dharma-treasury of the Buddha; one who upholds the Dharma will necessarily attain understanding.
Rāhula practices secret conduct; such conduct arises from understanding. Therefore, he also served as the eldest son of that Buddha. When conduct arises, understanding vanishes. Thus...

After that Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, Rāhula attained Buddhahood. Through the practice of understanding, he brought understanding to fruition; through the practice of conduct, he brought conduct to fruition.

This represents the mutual support of these two aspects. Those of superior capacity in his previous lives, those of middling capacity such as Kāśyapa and others, and those of inferior capacity numbering twelve hundred—those whose understanding and practice reside beyond these three capacities—are in fact unified and subsumed by him. Two thousand learners (śaikṣas) followed after him.
Regarding those who have attained the prediction [of enlightenment]: three faculties constitute the noble ones, while two thousand constitute the ordinary beings.

Whether noble or ordinary, they are all governed by understanding and practice; therefore, they abide within this [teaching]. Now, both understanding and practice are inherently present within one's own mind and do not come from without.
Once one has faith that one’s own mind attains Buddhahood, who would not give rise to understanding? Once understanding has arisen, who would not engage in cultivation? For this reason...
To understand without practicing puts the realization of the fruit far away; to understand and practice simultaneously, attainment occurs in an instant.
Śāriputra and the Dragon Girl clearly illustrate this difference in speed.

In the preceding "Chapter on the Dharma Master," a certain class of śrāvakas was recorded; thus, the gathering of those to be converted was not yet universal. Herein, the eight classes of beings—humans and non-humans alike—are recorded in detail, so that the benefit bestowed becomes complete.
Furthermore, the meaning of the previous seven chapters concerns hearing the Dharma in the past, receiving and upholding it, practicing it, and making offerings to it.

Regarding the attainment of the prediction (*vyākaraṇa*): those in this chapter who hear, uphold, practice, and make offerings to the Dharma in the present and future do so with the intention of propagating the sūtra;
therefore, they are designated as "Dharma Masters" (*dharmabhāṇaka*). Previously, during the time when the Buddha was in the world, they heard, upheld, and practiced the Dharma;

because the teacher was superior, the disciples were also superior. Herein, after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, they hear, uphold, and practice the Dharma; among humans, there is thus a distinction between the noble (*ārya*) and the ordinary (*pṛthagjana*).
Inferior. Since, within the Dharma, there is fundamentally no duality of "before" and "after," they are all equally granted the prediction [of enlightenment].

As for the full reception and upholding [of the teaching], whether it be a single phrase or a single verse, while there may appear to be a difference in terms of the extent of the text, there is no distinction in terms of the meaning;
therefore, they are all equally sent forth by the Tathāgata. These messengers do not come from minor merit; they have already made offerings to ten trillion [Buddhas].
The Buddha has accomplished his great vows and, out of compassion for sentient beings, was born into this human world;

therefore, he shall attain Buddhahood in the future and is one whom all people in the world ought to revere. He should be honored with the same offerings as a Tathāgata. To respect the master is to respect his servant;
yet a servant relies on the master’s majesty, so to treat a servant with contempt is worse than treating the master with contempt. Therefore, [the Buddha] was reviled before him.
The Buddha said: "The fault of that person is still light; however, the fault of one who slanders a holder of this sutra is even more grave. This sutra is none other than one's own mind.
In the teachings of the Buddhas from beginning to middle to end, there are none that do not point back to the realization of Buddhahood within one's own mind as their fundamental intent.

If one hears that Buddhahood is realized within one's own mind, even while the Tathāgata is present, many will still harbor resentment and jealousy—just as Śāriputra was filled with doubt upon first hearing it."
Even those who act as Māras harbor fear and trepidation in their hearts; how much more so, after my parinirvāṇa, would one not slander upon hearing this teaching?
If one can truly have self-confidence and be free from doubt, although one has not yet attained realization, one has already surpassed the three vehicles.

One’s attainment of Buddhahood is not far off, just as seeing damp earth makes one know that water must be near—surpassing the high plateau. Yet, while self-confidence is still relatively easy, acting for the sake of others is even more difficult; therefore, I entrust this to you.
It possesses the three matters of the Tathāgata; indeed, a single phrase is no different from the entire text, and my humble discourse does not differ from its broad exposition.

Dwelling in this evil world, one cannot be without reliance. Just as when the One Who Is Not Disparaging (Adhimātra-nirdeśa) recited a single phrase of the sutra, the fourfold assembly struck and pelted him with sticks, wood, tiles, and stones;
yet he still fled far away to dwell there, loudly proclaiming: "I do not dare to disparage..."
"You all, you shall all become Buddhas. Because they possess three things, comparing that [teaching] with this, one knows it to be of vital importance.
(From the "Chapter on the Appearance of the Jeweled Stūpa")
The preceding passage employed provisional language and metaphors, each instance pointing directly to the self-mind of the practitioner.

Fearing that they might still lack faith—exalting the realm of the sages while resigning themselves to being excluded from it—the text borrows the manifestation of the stupa of Prabhūtaratna as proof. The "Jeweled Stupa" is the physical body (*rūpakāya*);
the Buddha within the stupa is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*). Its height of five hundred *yojanas* signifies its vertical transcendence of the five stages; its breadth...
Its breadth of two hundred and fifty *yojanas* signifies its horizontal extension across the twenty-five realms of existence (*bhava*).
Its emergence from the earth signifies its emergence from the ground of ignorance (*avidyā*). Its dwelling in mid-air means that it does not rely upon the heavens above nor cling to the earth below.

One dwells in accordance with the Middle Way of the true nature (*dharmatā*). The principle of the true nature is signless (*animitta*) yet not non-signless; therefore, it does not obstruct its various adornments.
The railings signify the meaning of the seat of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); the grotto signifies the meaning of the chamber of compassion (*karuṇā-garbha*);
and the banners and streamers are made of brocade and silk, soft and fluttering, which signify the meaning of the robe of patience (*kṣānti-cīvara*). All three of these—
This is the virtue of one’s own mind. It does not hinder the adornment of various wholesome qualities;

thus, like a jeweled necklace with tinkling bells, the four analytical knowledges (*catasraḥ pratisaṃvidah*) are loftily suspended to widely proclaim the sublime Dharma. As the sound of the Dharma spreads far and wide, the fragrance of its virtue is heard from afar;
therefore, sandalwood incense issues forth from all four directions. To endure hardships while propagating the sutras, taking compassion as the foremost principle, is like a banner having a canopy.
Loving-kindness and forbearance must be accomplished through a multitude of meritorious deeds; therefore, they are composed of gold, silver, lapis lazuli, and other such materials.
All beings of the four modes of birth possess this mind; thus, it extends upward as far as the palaces of the Four Heavenly Kings, where each cultivates pure karma to adorn this mind.
Therefore, white flowers rained from the heavens as an offering to the jeweled stūpa. All beings of diverse kinds did not fail to adorn this mind together;
thus, there were further devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of supernatural beings who raised offerings. The sound produced by the stūpa was like the sound of a living body.
Praising Śākyamuni is like the mouth preaching the Dharma. Mahāpratibhāna’s request signifies the great eloquence that extensively proclaims the treatise which clarifies one’s own mind.
The presence of the whole body within the jeweled stupa signifies that sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata.
"The past" refers to what precedes; "the eastern direction" refers to the locus of movement. What precedes is stillness.
To the east, there was movement. This mind is neither still nor moving; therefore, he again passed through immeasurable thousands of myriads of koṭis of asaṃkhyeya worlds.
Because the jewel of the mind of true reality (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is pure and stainless, the land is named Ratnaviśuddha.

Because the pure true reality gives birth to all the jewels of the Dharma, the Buddha’s name is Prabhūtaratna. As for those who have made great vows, they have resolved their minds to propagate [the teaching].
It is a sutra. "After his parinirvāṇa" refers to attaining the realization of the true mark (dharmatā). "Distantly testifying to the preaching of the Dharma" means fulfilling one's original vow.
"The fourfold assembly desiring to see his entire body" expresses their hope for his manifestation. "Causing the emanated bodies to assemble" means gathering and subduing the deluded mind.
"Transforming the pure land three times before the appearance of Prabhūtaratna" signifies the exhaustion of delusion and the perfection of awakening.

The two Buddhas being together within the stupa signifies the harmonious integration of the provisional and the ultimate. The great assembly all dwelling together in mid-air signifies their collective realization of the true mark (*dharmatā*).
Since they all go to witness and certify wherever the *Lotus Sūtra* is preached, how could this not be a certification of what was previously received?

The bestowal of predictions is entirely a manifestation of one's own mind; it is certainly not something bestowed from without. Long ago, there was a monk sitting cross-legged on a bridge who heard [the sound of the sūtra].
The two ghosts conversed with one another. One ghost said, "I hope that tomorrow someone will come to relieve me. The other ghost asked, "What is that person like?
He replied, "One who wears an iron hat. A monk heard this and waited; he saw a man walking through the rain with a cauldron on his head, going beneath a bridge to wash his feet.
The monk told him the reason and stopped him. The ghost said resentfully, "What kind of bald thing is this? He has ruined my—"
This was a favorable circumstance. [The monk] vowed to harm the monks. The monks withdrew their thoughts and entered meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

The ghost said, "How strange! Why do I see only a jeweled stupa and not the person? After a long while, the monk formed this thought: "The ghost must surely depart. The ghost said, "He comes! He comes!

The monk again withdrew his thoughts. This occurred three times. Then, suddenly and completely, he attained great enlightenment. People of the time called this "Chan induced by the pressure of a ghost."
Master, by this reasoning, you will know that my statement that the jeweled stupa is the physical body itself is not without basis.
Furthermore, when a single thought is withdrawn, not only can ghosts not see it, but even a Buddha cannot perceive it. This can be personally verified in one's daily life.
What need is there to seek for kalpas? Failing to understand how to settle the mind, others have caused the Buddhas to labor with manifold instructions.
Our Original Teacher has now revealed this clearly and openly, without further concealment; you should believe it deeply. Thus is the realization established, and the task is complete.
Therefore, in the verses, he extensively clarifies that this sutra is difficult to uphold, and praises those who uphold it, thereby opening [the teaching].
The intent of this dissemination is as follows:

in the section preceding the "Devadatta Chapter," [the Buddha] earnestly exhorted the bhikṣus to endure hardships and propagate the sutra, desiring that their life of wisdom (prajñā-jīvita) remain uninterrupted.
Therefore, although there may be those who propagate the sutras, if there are none who seek the Dharma, what benefit is there in propagating it?

Thus, the example of the Wheel-Turning King seeking the Dharma is cited to awaken the minds of those in the末世 (mòshì, final age). Furthermore, as for the Wheel-Turning King, he is the sovereign among men, his nobility peerless;
yet he still cast aside his arrogance and sovereignty, and when there was one who preached the Dharma, he willingly became a servant, attending to and making offerings to him, humbling himself.
From this point downward, who among them would not seek the Dharma? However, there are two essentials for seeking the Dharma: first, one must not observe their conduct;
second, one must not observe their lineage. Regarding not observing conduct: take Devadatta, for example.
He was the Buddha’s malicious adversary throughout many lifetimes, yet the Buddha said that it was due to Devadatta as a "good spiritual friend" (kalyāṇamitra) [that he attained enlightenment].
Therefore, it causes me to fulfill the six pāramitās, up to the powers of the divine path, to achieve equal and perfect enlightenment, and to extensively deliver all sentient beings.
This is the sign of turning adversity into favor. Shun was called "Greatly Filial" because his parents brought it to completion.
The Immortal’s forbearance was perfected by King Li. The integrity of the pine and cypress is revealed in the severity of frost and snow. [The blade...]
The sharpness of a sword depends on the hardness of the whetstone; wood becomes a ridgepole or a beam because of the artisan’s chisel;
and gold attains its purity through the intensity of fire. Whether sentient or insentient, all things are accomplished through adverse conditions. Therefore it is said:
Goodness is easy to practice yet difficult to ascend; evil is difficult to dwell upon yet easy to fall into. This depends solely on the wise person’s skillful observation. Thus Yongjia said:
"To observe malicious words as a source of merit is what constitutes my spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*).

By not giving rise to enmity or kinship because of slander, how can this fail to manifest the power of non-arising compassion and patience? Inferring from this, [the Buddha] descended from the Tuṣita Heaven...
Those who hear the Dharma from Bha are situated amidst adverse conditions. It is precisely through these adverse conditions that one accomplishes the bodhi of a person;

therefore, at the time of attaining Buddhahood, he is titled "Heavenly King" (*Devarāja*). Because his majestic power compels others, he possesses the sovereignty of a heavenly king. Thus, the world is named the "Way of Heaven.
This is like the autumn season, which is stern and destructive toward all things, yet all things depend upon it for their growth and emergence—this too is an adverse condition.
Regarding the meaning of accomplishing conditions: although the Tathāgata acted as the primary figure here, he was in fact exhorting future generations.
For those who seek the Dharma in later times often retreat due to adverse conditions, such as when Śāriputra begged for his eyes.

If one can remain ever compliant amidst adversity, then there is no dharma that cannot become a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*). As for not observing one's spiritual lineage (*gotra*), this is clarified by means of the dragon girl.
This is the matter. Prabhūtaratna is the essence (*tattva*) of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), while Jñatikūṭa is the function (*vṛtti*) of the true mark.
Śākyamuni’s refusal of [Prabhūtaratna’s] request to return to his own land is the symbol of withdrawing function back into essence.

Śākyamuni’s refusal to permit him to depart and his instruction that he must instead discuss and clarify the wondrous Dharma with Mañjuśrī is the symbol of not abandoning the great function. Mañjuśrī, together with countless bodhisattvas, [departed] from...
Regarding "emerging from the great ocean": this is a metaphor for the fact that all wisdom and conduct arise from the ocean of the mind.

Since they both equally emerge from the ocean of the mind, how can there be any distinction between the noble and the ordinary, or any division between humans and nāgas? Because they cannot be divided.
That very class of beings, the nāgas, practiced the bodhisattva path. Now, nāgas are of a different species; she was not a man.

She was eight years old, not of venerable age; her practice lasted but a moment, not a long time. That she attained Buddhahood by offering a single pearl in a single thought-moment clarifies that she understood the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
As for her necessarily attaining Buddhahood in the south: the south corresponds to the trigram *Li*, which is the symbol of the empty mind. It is emptiness.
The mind has no realization, yet there is nothing it does not realize; thus, the marks and signs of excellence and the supernormal powers are all accomplished in dependence upon it.
That the fourfold assembly all pay homage and respect is because, as it is said, "there is no discrimination regarding spiritual lineage.
When the dragon girl offered a pearl in a single thought and immediately attained perfect enlightenment, how could we possibly abandon ourselves and fail to believe?

In the "Chapter on Upholding" (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*) and the "Chapter on the Jeweled Stupa" (*Stūpa-saṃdarśana-parivarta*), the Buddha deeply praises those who uphold this sutra. Furthermore, in the "Chapter on Devadatta" (*Devadatta-parivarta*), he exhorts seekers of the Dharma to exhaust their utmost sincerity.
Therefore, the twenty thousand bodhisattvas, including Bhaiṣajyarāja and others, profoundly grasped the Buddha’s intention and made vows to uphold this sutra, even in the final age.

"The sentient beings of this world are stubborn and difficult to transform. We have aroused the power of great patience; what need is there to worry about their wickedness, arrogance, anger, turbidity, and deceit?
Furthermore, there are five hundred śrāvakas and eight thousand learners who, although they have received predictions of enlightenment, have not yet perfected their power of patience;
therefore, they vow to uphold this sutra in other lands. The bhikṣuṇī Mahāprajāpatī, however, clings to the past..."

Regarding the provisional teaching: she previously disparaged her own female body, deeming it not a vessel for the Dharma; though she heard that the śrāvakas receive predictions of enlightenment, she still doubted that she herself was beyond such a destiny.
Only now, seeing the dragon girl attain Buddhahood, has she first given rise to this aspiration and hopes for a prediction. It is for this reason that the Buddha rebukes her.
I have previously stated in general that all śrāvakas have already received their predictions of enlightenment. At that time, there was no distinction made between men and women;
what is it that you do not understand, such that you continue to harbor lingering attachment? The Buddha’s name is Sarvasattvapriyadarśana (He Who Is Seen with Joy by All Beings).
Pajāpatī means "Great Path of Love" (Mahāmāyā); because she loved the Path during her causal stage, when she attained the fruit, people likewise rejoiced.
It is so seen. Yaśodharā shall become a Buddha named "Endowed with Myriad Myriads of Radiant Marks.

Because she was the wife of the Bodhisattva, the wife symbolizes the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*). Being "endowed with myriad myriads of radiant marks" is the manifestation of this joy of the Dharma.

As for the aforementioned Bodhisattvas such as Bhaiṣajyarāja and others who have made vows to uphold this sutra in this land, as well as the five hundred śrāvakas and eight thousand learners (*śaikṣa*), they have taken their oaths.

If one were to request others in other lands to uphold the sutra, there would be a distinction between "this" and "that," and thus it would not be universal. Therefore, the World-Honored One gazed upon eighty quadrillion nayutas of bodhisattvas;
his intention was for them to propagate and uphold [the teaching] everywhere. Since he desired them to propagate and uphold it, why did he not issue a clear command?

It is because one must personally resolve their own mind for the practice to be truly intimate and effective. Thus, the various bodhisattvas, out of reverence and in accordance with the Buddha's intention, acted...
The Lion’s Roar: Making the vow to travel throughout the worlds of the ten directions after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa to uphold this sutra.
The Chapter on Peaceful Conduct.
The Bodhisattvas such as Medicine King and others previously made vows to endure hardships and uphold this sutra in the final age.

Since there is already a mind capable of endurance and an object toward which that endurance is directed, the subject and object stand in mutual dependence; how could there not be hardships? It would be better, therefore, to distance oneself from suspicion and to know how to avoid what is forbidden.

If one brings about the absence of difficulties, then there will be no patience required to endure anything, and one will attain peace and happiness. The sphere of practice for a Bodhisattva consists precisely of the aforementioned three dharmas.
"Abiding on the ground of patience" carries the meaning of the robe of patience. "Gentle, harmonious, and compliant," and so forth, carry the meaning of the chamber of compassion and loving-kindness.
"Having no practice regarding phenomena," and so forth, carry the meaning of the seat of the emptiness of phenomena. Although the Bodhisattva practices this personal peace and happiness...
One should not seek to be known by others; naturally, people will cherish one’s virtue, revere it, and draw near. Once people have drawn near, it becomes easy for other matters to arise;
therefore, this is followed by the section on "Places to Avoid Drawing Near," so that one may know what to choose and not fall into various difficulties.

If one draws near to kings and the like, arrogance easily arises; if one draws near to non-Buddhists and the like, false views easily grow; and if one draws near to those who engage in worldly affairs...

Regarding literary composition and the like: one fears they will obstruct right practice; one fears that associating with *caṇḍālas* will give rise to evil thoughts; one fears that associating with *śrāvakas* will cause one to fall into the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*);

and one fears that associating with women will give rise to lustful thoughts. These are all things one should not associate with. To sit in meditation in a secluded place and contemplate the emptiness of all phenomena—this is what one should associate with.
This is the cultivation of bodily action (*kāyakarman*). In the Dharma-ending age, spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) may follow the path or go against it.

The accomplishment of sentient beings is inconceivable. Whether through the Great or Small Teachings, or by the suppression or exaltation of the provisional or the real, each accords with what is appropriate for the time;

therefore, one should never speak of their faults. Should there be those who pose difficult questions or objections, one should simply teach according to the Mahāyāna and not respond with the Hīnayāna.
This is the cultivation of verbal karma. Let jealousy not disturb the mind; let contempt not pass through the heart; let thoughts of others' shortcomings not take shape in one's reflections.
Accord with the Three Vehicles and preach the Dharma according to the capacities of beings, so that they are neither troubled nor doubtful. Seeking the supreme above and transforming those below:
do not trouble them by speaking of their laxity and indolence; do not cause them doubt by saying they cannot attain the Knowledge of All Modes (sarvākārajñatā). Above...
When seeking [the Dharma], one conceives of the Tathāgata as a compassionate father and the Bodhisattva as a great teacher.

When transforming those below, one preaches the Dharma with equanimity, neither too much nor too little; this is the cultivation of mental action (*manas-karman*). Although the superior [practitioner] fully cultivates the three types of action, they focus primarily on self-benefit.

The inferior [practitioner], however, separately cultivates loving-kindness and compassion, focusing primarily on benefiting others. Because they cultivate great loving-kindness, toward householders and renunciants...
Among one's family members, one teaches the Dharma with an impartial mind, causing them to obtain benefit and happiness by cultivating great compassion.

Toward those who are not bodhisattvas or those who lack faith, one makes a vow to teach the Dharma, enabling them to attain liberation. Furthermore, this Dharma of peace and happiness, when opened up, consists of four practices.

It should be understood that through the perfection of both compassion and wisdom, one becomes an object of veneration and respect for the fourfold assembly, while the devas and other beings attend upon and protect one.
This sutra is the subtle and wondrous nature of one's own mind, the very foundation of all Buddhas;

therefore, it is likened to the jewel within the topknot of a universal monarch (*cakravartin*). The noble ones of the three vehicles have partially realized their own minds, yet they have not fully exhausted its wondrousness.
It is like the distribution of various rewards: when ordinary beings have a single thought of self-confidence, they immediately receive a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
Yet the noble ones (*ārya*) give rise to doubt, as if the king’s retinue were struck with wonder. That one's own mind is the Buddha is the foremost teaching of all Buddhas.

That one attains Buddhahood through one's own mind is, among all teachings, the most profound, difficult to believe, and difficult to understand. Even while the Tathāgata is present, there are still many who harbor resentment.
How much less would those of the icchantika class harbor resentment or slander, or create obstacles and difficulties, after my parinirvāṇa?
If one can cultivate these four kinds of peace and happiness, then one will be revered by the fourfold assembly in daily life and shall see wondrous things in dreams.
What cause for concern is there that beings of stubborn nature are difficult to transform? How could it be said that the bodhisattva’s practice is difficult to perform?

Regarding the "Chapter on the Emergence from the Earth," the fact that the Buddha did not grant permission to the bodhisattvas from other lands who wished to protect and uphold this sutra serves to manifest the provisional teachings and skillful means (*upāya*).

Within these provisional teachings, names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) are established in great abundance; therefore, it is said to exceed the number of sands in eight *gaṅgā-nadī* rivers by way of skillful means.
Names and marks are all termed external objects. Where there are external objects, there is internal mind; with the opposition of subject and object, how could one protect the sutra?
Therefore, I have ceased [this discussion]. In my Sahā world, there are naturally bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of sixty thousand Ganges Rivers.

This refers to the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*). The fact that each Bodhisattva has a retinue of sixty thousand *gaṅgā-nadī-vāluka* (Ganges sands) signifies the mutual functioning of the six organs and the manifestation of their respective manifold merits.
As the *Śūraṃgama-sūtra* states: "If the six organs did not function interchangeably..."
Then, by what means can you uproot the fundamental root of your beginningless deluded thoughts?

Know that the protection and maintenance of this sutra depend upon the mutual functioning of one's own six sense faculties. Those who emerge from the earth likewise emerge from the ground of ignorance.
Regarding "dwelling in the space below": this means that all six sense faculties dwell within the Middle Way of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore, "below" refers to the earth. Earth is the symbol of *kūn* (the trigram for earth); *kūn* represents the way of flexibility, which signifies gentleness and patience. "Above" refers to heaven;
heaven is able to cover all things, which signifies the universal covering of compassion. "Space" refers to the meaning of the emptiness of all phenomena (*sarvadharma-śūnyatā*). From [this point]...
Because these six sense organs are endowed with three dharmas, they are able to protect and uphold this sutra; it is not something that external objects can protect.
Regarding the Bodhisattvas from sixty thousand down to four, three, two, and one: "one" is a symbol for the immeasurable.
Being alone without retinue signifies that their number exceeds the aforementioned; "one" here is a symbol for the immeasurable. As for those who dwell in mid-air:
This abides in the Middle Way. Because the Middle Way does not obstruct the provisional and the real, each [bodhisattva] proceeds to the void to pay homage at the feet of the two World-Honored Ones.
Relying on the provisional and the real, they do not abandon the affairs of response and transformation; thus, they again turn toward the Transformation Buddha to pay homage.
To clarify the awakening to one’s own mind is to destroy ignorance; therefore, the earth everywhere quakes and splits open, and [the bodhisattvas] emerge from within it. Since ignorance has been...
When [the delusions] are shattered, one transcends the five aggregates in a single moment; thus, fifty minor kalpas are perceived by the great assembly as being like half a day.

Relying on the realization of one’s own mind, one fully realizes that both the sense faculties and their objects are identical to the true mark (dharmatā). Consequently, one sees all bodhisattvas filling the void.
Although these bodhisattvas are vast and beyond counting, they are headed by four types of peaceful bliss. Their bodies reside in...

Because it precedes the three types of karma, it is called "Superior Conduct" (Urdhvagāminī-caryā). Because the mouth is able to preach the Dharma with eloquent expression and inexhaustible principle, it is called "Boundless Conduct" (Anantā-caryā).
Because one has realized the defiled nature of one's own mind and thereby attained purity, it is called "Pure Conduct" (Śuddhā-caryā).
Because establishing all sentient beings cannot be accomplished without great compassion, it is called "Establishing Conduct" (Pratiṣṭhāpanā-caryā). Thus do Bodhisattvas revere [it].

When he inquired after the World-Honored One’s well-being, and the World-Honored One replied with words of well-being, this was to verify the meaning of his prior intention to protect himself through well-being.

Next, when he asked whether sentient beings were easy to transform and guide, the World-Honored One likewise answered that they were easy to transform and guide, further adding that they would "constantly receive my transformation throughout successive lifetimes.
This was to secretly reveal the meaning of the Buddha's lifespan. Upon hearing these words regarding sentient beings throughout the ages, the Bodhisattva...
Since those in the world have been transformed by the Buddha, it is known that they can easily be delivered; thus, they give rise to a mind of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*).

Although Maitreya and the eight thousand *gaṅgā*-sands of bodhisattvas, within the "Introductory Chapter," realized that past and present are but a single thought-moment and understood that the causal mind is thus, they still believed that the fruit of Buddhahood must necessarily be attained through cultivation, not realizing that their attainment of Buddhahood had already occurred long ago. Therefore...
They gave rise to doubts and asked questions; even the attendants of the transformation Buddhas likewise gave rise to doubts and addressed the Buddha.

This was to demonstrate that the wisdom of skillful means cannot encompass the fundamental lifespan of the fruit-virtue. The Buddha told them, "Maitreya has already questioned you, and it is because of this that you have been able to hear [this teaching].
This matter can only be fully realized through the wisdom of an Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi). The Buddha intended to clearly reveal the distant [truth].
Fundamentally, one must first strengthen their faith; therefore, I have exhorted them to don the armor of diligence and to resolve with firm intent.

When you asked, "By whom were these bodhisattvas taught? From whom did they resolve to attain enlightenment? What Buddha-dharma did they proclaim? I replied: "I am their teacher; from me they resolved to attain enlightenment;
it is my Way and Dharma that they proclaimed. When you asked, "In what land do they dwell? I replied: "It is this very Sahā world. As for your further question...
"From where have you come? "I have come from the space below. "Which sutra do you maintain and uphold?
"I have read and recited the *Svabhāva-sūtra* until I am thoroughly proficient in it. "Why do you say that you do not recognize a single person?
"These bodhisattvas do not delight in being among the many or in much talk; they always delight in solitary places and do not dwell relying upon humans or devas. Furthermore, this..."
Bodhisattvas are entirely the quiescent light and the true mark (*dharmatā*); they are not objects known by the mind or consciousness.

As stated previously, Śāriputra was taught by twenty thousand Buddhas during the aeon prior to the "dust-point" kalpa, when he served as the Dharma-preacher for the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*. Thus, the remoteness of his teaching and transformation is as clear as this.
For what reason does Maitreya again rely on recent traces to challenge the distant origin? This is because the preceding text has already elucidated it.

Generally speaking, while the preceding discussion concerned the cause, this present inquiry and refutation focus exclusively on the fruit. This is because those of the Three Vehicles know only the long duration of traversing the causes, but do not know that they have been Buddhas from the very beginning.

Traversing the causes and attaining realization occurs at the level of the *saṃbhogakāya* (retribution body), whereas being a Buddha from the beginning occurs at the level of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).
Since the former involves traversing the causes and attaining realization, there are the analogies of the three carts and the single cart; herein [the latter is addressed].

The traces are opened to reveal the fundamental; thus, the father is young while the son is old is used as a metaphor. The reward body (*vipākakāya*) is a proximate realization, fully endowed with adornments, and is therefore said to be "young.
The Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is primordial, not subject to birth or extinction, and has already perfected the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa*);

therefore, it is said to be "old. The son dwells in the Land of Quiescent Light, while the father resides in the land of reward; thus, those of the Three Vehicles do not recognize them as one person. Herein, the Tathāgata reveals and clarifies this quiescence.
The light and the land of recompense are without difference; therefore, it is said that this is beneath the Sahā world. The Dharma-body and the Recompense-body are of one essence;
therefore, it is said that these are those whom I have taught and transformed. This chapter reveals the traces (*jì*), while the following chapter manifests the fundamental reality (*běn*).
These traces and the fundamental reality do not transcend one's own mind. If the mind lingers upon distant causes, then even through vast eons they will be difficult to accomplish. If the mind can...

Through sudden enlightenment, one attains Buddhahood prior to the kalpas as numerous as atoms in a buddha-field. Thus it is said: "Without leaving Tuṣita, he has already descended into the royal palace;
without emerging from the mother's womb, his work of saving sentient beings is complete."

In the "Life Span of the Tathāgata" chapter, Maitreya bases his argument on the traces of the recent past at Gayā to challenge the fundamental reality; the Tathāgata relies upon the fundamental fruit of the *jigguang* (tranquil light) realm to refute those traces.
This is intended to lead future students to each awaken to their own original portion (*bun*) and thereby sever all external longing; thus, father and son open [the teaching].
The reason for the repeated exhortations is that this Dharma is profound, difficult to believe, and difficult to understand;
therefore, it is repeatedly admonished and encouraged to strengthen one’s faith. Maitreya and the others, grasping the Buddha’s intention, likewise requested instruction three times.
The World-Honored One first acknowledged their difficulty and subsequently revealed the fundamental [truth], saying: "You all..."
It is said that I attained the Way recently at Gayā; how could you know that in reality I have been a Buddha for kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, beyond all comparison?

Furthermore, you see only me attaining enlightenment at Gayā, yet you do not know that I have attained enlightenment and preached the Dharma to benefit sentient beings in hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of asamkhyeya lands. You do not even know my traces.
How much more so regarding its fundamental source? Such manifestations are not unique to me; all Buddhas are likewise.
Therefore, when I speak of past Buddhas such as Dīpaṃkara attaining enlightenment and now having entered parinirvāṇa, these are all provisional proclamations of their traces.

If one discusses their fundamental source, how could it ever transcend a single thought-moment? Since this is so, why not directly reveal the fundamental mind instead of speaking of provisional means?

This trace is, in essence, one's own fundamental mind. Although it is fully possessed by every person, because they have wandered for a long time, their delusion and estrangement have deepened day by day, resulting in distinctions among faculties such as sharp or dull, and great or small. Thus, the Tathāgata universally observes the capacities of all beings.
He tames beings according to what is necessary for their deliverance; therefore, there are various names and numerous teachings.
Even such things as manifesting birth, manifesting renunciation, appearing to attain enlightenment, or entering parinirvāṇa are all skillful means (*upāya*).
Since skillful means are fundamentally intended to lead toward the reality, none of the sūtras he has taught fail to cause sentient beings to [attain liberation].
They enter the Buddha-way. Thus, whether he speaks of his own body or the bodies of others, all such statements are true and not false.

When it is said that the Tathāgata knows and perceives the characteristics of the triple world as they truly are, and that there is no birth-and-death or coming-and-going, this means that although the Tathāgata exists within the triple world, he does not participate in the arising and ceasing of the triple world.
If the Tathāgata were identical to the triple world, [he would likewise be subject to birth and death].
Consequently, one would be unable to perfectly mirror their existence in the world, their extinction, their birth-and-death, and their transcendence.
Because these states are not identical, regarding the coming and going of birth-and-death and the extinction within the world as either the same or different would result in a flawed understanding.

Because of this perfect mirroring, one clearly perceives that all sentient beings each possess the fundamental essence; yet, being shrouded by ignorance, they manifest various dispositions and desires.
...these differences. He further employs various causes and conditions and various parables to skillfully guide their minds, causing them to become sons of the Buddha.
Yet, even the lifespan achieved by the Tathāgata while practicing the bodhisattva path during his causal stage was already immeasurable;
how much more so the lifespan of the originally inherent fruit-body? To speak of attaining enlightenment and entering nirvana is like a skilled physician—
This is for the purpose of treating mad children. Because the Tathāgata is fully endowed with the four wisdoms, he is said to be "wise and sagacious.

Because he well knows the distinct characteristics of the various scriptures and teachings, he is said to be "expert in prescriptions and medicines. Because he can resolve all the afflictions of sentient beings, he is said to be "skilled in curing all ailments.
Since those of the three vehicles and five natures are all sons of the Buddha, he is said to have "many children. This method...
Because his karmic capacity had ceased and the conditions for other lands had matured, it is said that "he went far to another country due to matters of business.

Since the Buddha had already passed into nirvana, sentient beings received and followed false teachings; thus, it is said that "they drank the poison of others. Having received false teachings, their grasping views increased.
Transmigrating through birth and death, it is said that "the medicine took effect, causing him to become dazed and roll upon the ground.

The Buddha contemplated how to rescue and deliver him, and thus returned to manifest birth, like an elder returning home. The fourfold assembly looked up to him with reverence, like children rejoicing;

he followed ancient precedents and intended to expound the Three Vehicles. Thus it is said: "Relying on the prescriptions of various scriptures, he sought excellent medicinal herbs and fully explained the three trainings."

Because it possesses the three qualities and other such attributes, it is said that "it is fully endowed with color, fragrance, and exquisite flavor. To examine this dharma-gate thoroughly and to provide instruction for its cultivation, it is said:
"Grind, sift, and mix it, then give it to the child to consume. If one can practice according to these instructions, one will then sever the afflictions (*kleśa*).
One departs from birth and death; hence it is said: "Swiftly eliminate suffering and affliction so that no further calamities remain.

Those who take the medicine and are cured of their illness represent those who have achieved realization in the present life. Those who, though pleased, do not take the medicine represent the class of those with overweening pride and indolence.

The arrival of old age and death signifies that the time for *nirvāṇa* is near. Leaving behind the medicine as a final instruction means entrusting [the teaching] to be compiled. Once again, he arrived.
"Other lands" refers to other regions. "Sending a messenger back to report" refers to the Bodhisattva’s proclamation of his parinirvāṇa.

"The son hearing this and becoming distressed" refers to the fourfold assembly’s sorrowful longing. "His mind awakening and submitting through reflection" refers to practicing in accordance with the teachings.

"The father returning once the illness has been cured" refers to the severing of delusions and the manifestation of principle. The sons merely see their father coming and going, and thus they themselves experience grief and joy.
How could one know that the father had not actually died? This clarifies that sentient beings see only the traces and forget the source.

One should know that the father is the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), while the sons are consciousness and perception (*vijñāna-saṃjñā*). The true mind is fundamentally unmoving; it is only through the deluded perceptions of consciousness and perception that coming and going are seen.
If these deluded perceptions are realized as empty, then from beginning to end there is no departure from the present moment. Trusting directly in this, we shall all attain Buddhahood.
For a long time, had you not accepted this responsibility, you would have been merely attributing credit to the Buddha alone.

Those in the "Chapter on the Differentiation of Merit" who heard of the Great Assembly that the Buddha’s lifespan is long and far-reaching and thereby obtained great benefit, each realized that their own minds are inherently endowed with such longevity.

This is the meaning of the fact that one’s life-span is originally and fundamentally the Buddha. The World-Honored One certified that what [the Bodhisattva] had attained was not erroneous; therefore, he addressed Maitreya and proclaimed it.

By hearing of the original life-span, one penetrates the realization that the three periods of time are a single thought-moment, thereby knowing that every phenomenon is unborn. Thus, one attains the patience of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Hearing of the Buddha’s original life-span, one awakens to the knowledge that all things arise from the fundamental source and follow along with it.
One should expound that all enter the Single Vehicle (Ekayāna). Thus, one attains the dhāraṇī-door of hearing and retaining.
Having thoroughly understood the Single Vehicle, one then clearly penetrates its distinctions and skillfully answers difficult questions; thus, one attains unimpeded eloquence (anāvaraṇa-pratibhāna).

One harmonizes these distinctions as being entirely the single mind of oneself, just as the whirlpools of the ocean cause the hundred rivers and myriad streams to become of one flavor; thus, one attains the *āvarta-dhāraṇī*.
Once the nun had awakened to her own mind, she realized that the Buddha, sentient beings, and the mind are non-differentiated in these three respects.

Since time immemorial, they have neither emerged nor vanished; thus, she turned the Dharma-wheel of non-retrogression. She realized that all distinctions are fundamentally one’s own mind, which is neither defiled nor pure;
thus, she turned the wheel of the pure Dharma. This describes the merit of her direct realization from the eighth birth onward.

Reaching the final birth, it describes that they shall attain Bodhi in the future. It further describes how sentient beings as numerous as the atoms in eight worlds all resolve their minds toward Bodhi.

Thus we know that although there are differences in the distance of time until one attains Buddhahood upon awakening to one's own mind, one will certainly not fall back into the stages of Śrāvaka or Pratyekabuddha.
The preceding passage’s exposition of the provisional to reveal the real has this meaning.

Because he was following the traces [of the Buddha], he bestowed predictions upon Śāriputra and two thousand others—both those in training (*śaikṣa*) and those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*)—that they would surely attain Buddhahood after the passage of immeasurable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas;
their numbers were specifically one thousand two hundred and two thousand, as such figures are generally known to the mind.

Herein, the traces are opened to reveal the fundamental reality; since the intent lies in the fundamental reality, he describes the actual merits realized by the various bodhisattvas, for attaining Buddhahood depends solely upon this.

There were those who had attained birth once and those who had attained birth eight times; their assembly numbered as many as the atoms of worlds. Among them were followers of the Three Vehicles, beyond all imagination.
When comparing their relative merits, the difference was more than that between heaven and abyss. Such spiritual benefits are rarely heard of in the world;

therefore, the heavens rained down precious flowers to celebrate them, further signifying that the entire great assembly had obtained wondrous causes. These flowers were scattered upon the lion throne and...
As for the Buddhas: the transformation-buddhas are those manifested by one's own mind, signifying that all dharmas of the Dharma possess their original life-span.
Furthermore, the inclusion of the Original Teacher and Prabhūtaratna within the scattered stūpas signifies that this fundamental fruit fully manifests both the provisional and the real.
Likewise, the scattering [of these] among all bodhisattvas and the fourfold assembly signifies that both ordinary beings and sages equally attain this Dharma. Incense rains down, and music resounds.
The scattering of robes and jewels is a symbol of the sudden realization that one’s own mind is replete with all virtues.
The fact that the necklaces pervade the nine directions signifies that sentient beings throughout the nine realms all possess these virtues.

The Bodhisattvas holding banners and canopies as far as the Brahma Heaven symbolizes that compassion and skillful means transcend all conditioned practices. [This was] bestowed within the section on the Gate of Prior Traces.

Commentary: One must practice all six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*) to attain Buddhahood. Yet, within this Root Chapter, by merely hearing once of the Buddha’s long life-span, one immediately attains supreme benefit and becomes fully endowed with the perfection of wisdom (*prajñā-pāramitā*).

This surpasses the merit of those who have practiced the other five perfections for eighty quadrillion (*nayuta*) nayutas of kalpas, thereby manifesting the extraordinary excellence of the Root Chapter. Why is it that by merely hearing once of the original life-span...
One immediately attains such benefits as these. Even one who has a slight understanding of the meaning of the words gives rise to the unsurpassed wisdom of the Tathāgata;
how much more so for one who hears extensively—how could such a person not obtain this benefit? To uphold the teachings oneself is wisdom; to fully cultivate offerings is merit.

When these two matters are fully perfected, one’s virtues become equal to those of the Buddha; therefore, one is able to give rise to the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). To briefly explain the meaning of this discourse:
once this is attained, if one can, with a profound mind, believe, understand, and realize that one’s own mind is such, then one will know that the Buddha-body fundamentally has no coming or going.

Thus, one sees that the single assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa is ever-present within the Sahā world, no different from the Flower Treasury World (*Puṣpasaṃbhava-kośa-lokadhātu*); thus, one beholds its ground.
It is adorned with various ornaments. Yet, while it was easier to believe in this sutra while the Buddha was in the world, it is even more difficult to believe in it after his parinirvāṇa.
Therefore, merely refraining from disparaging it and giving rise to a mind of sympathetic joy constitutes the mark of deep faith and understanding.
Since this sutra is the dharmakāya of all Buddhas, those who uphold it are thereby honoring the Tathāgata upon their heads. This sutra is indeed one...

Because he embodies the Three Jewels, one who makes offerings to him has already established stupas, temples, and monastic quarters. Although this is explained from the perspective of principle (*li*), principle does not contradict phenomena (*shi*).
Furthermore, it clarifies that one who upholds this sutra concurrently practices the six perfections and constructs monasteries and the like;

since both principle and phenomena are thus complete, the attainment of Buddhahood is a matter of but a single moment (*kṣaṇa*). Therefore, it is said that one swiftly reaches all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) and has already proceeded to the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Such a person is close to Bodhi; in their four modes of conduct, they enjoy the same as the Buddha.
How could one not erect a stupa for them, scatter flowers, and make offerings?

In the "Chapter on Rejoicing in Merit," the preceding chapter merely clarified the merit of hearing of the Tathāgata’s original lifespan and briefly explaining the profound intent of his words with deep faith and understanding;
it did not yet address the merit of rejoicing upon hearing the sutra after the Tathāgata’s parinirvāṇa, nor of subsequently expounding it for others and exhorting them to listen. Therefore—
This is a further clarification. The first person is the Tathāgata; the second person is a disciple of the Buddha; the third person is a teacher of the Semblance Dharma;
the fourth person is a member of the assembly; and the fifth person is one who hears it by way of oral transmission along the road.
Thus it is passed on in succession until the fiftieth person. Since the transmission has traveled so far, what is received becomes increasingly diminished, yet it still surpasses the mundane world.
If this is so for those of the Two Vehicles, how much more so for those at the very beginning? Furthermore, four million billion *asaṃkhyeya* worlds are not merely a single land;
the twelve classes of living beings are not merely the path of a single person; and eighty full years are not merely a single day or month.
Furthermore, they cause them to attain the Noble Vehicle, not merely the pleasures of the mundane world. Such giving of both material wealth and the Dharma is already inconceivable;
yet it still does not equal the merit of the fiftieth person who hears a single four-line verse and rejoices in it.

Indeed, this sutra is one's own mind. To be able to believe that one’s own mind can attain Buddhahood—though not yet realized—is already to transcend both the mundane and supramundane worlds by a vast distance, for one’s own mind is the Single Buddha Vehicle (*ekayāna*).
By listening and receiving it for even a moment, one immediately obtains the supreme and wondrous vehicle.
Since the mind is the sovereign of all things and the king of all phenomena, I urge people to sit and listen; I even share my seat with them.

By sitting there, one immediately attains the seat of Brahmā, Śakra, or a Cakravartin King. One encourages others to go and listen, thereby attaining rebirth in the same realm as the Bodhisattvas who possess *dhāraṇī*.

With keen faculties and wisdom, even to the point of the six sense organs becoming pure and sublime, those who see the Buddha and hear the Dharma encourage others to surely praise the wondrous Dharma; it is fitting that they obtain such retribution, even for a mere moment.
To listen and receive [the teaching], one cannot wait for a long duration; if one shares a seat and asks another to sit, it will be difficult to remain until the end of the session.

Therefore, rather than merely encouraging others to go and listen, it is better to hear it oneself. Since the merit is such even in this inferior case, the superior case can be understood accordingly.
For this reason, the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, though unable to widely propagate the teaching by his own power, merely held to a single phrase: "All of you..."
One should resolve to become a Buddha, personally upholding this [teaching] and encouraging others to do so; thereby, one transcends hundreds of thousands of kalpas and swiftly attains Bodhi.
How could the merit of such sympathetic joy (anumodanā) be compared to that of the two vehicles or the fields of merit of humans and devas?

In the preceding "Chapter on the Merits of the Dharma Master," the text describes how those who understand and accept through the three faculties, as well as those who extensively uphold even a single phrase or a single verse, all receive predictions of enlightenment and are fit to serve as models for humans and devas;
therefore, it specifically designates them as "Dharma Masters. Herein, the merit of sympathetic joy has already transcended that of both ordinary beings and sages. If...

Regarding those who fully receive and uphold [the teaching], what are their merits? It is clarified that they have already attained the purity of the six sense faculties; therefore, they are linked with these merits.

If this is so, since Arhats have already attained the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*) and the three types of clear knowledge (*tisro vidyāḥ*), they too are called "pure in the six sense faculties.

Why, then, would they not surpass the merit of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*)? This is because the Arhat abides in the fruit (*phala*), whereas upholding the sutra abides in the cause (*hetu*). Therefore, he...

Although they possess supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), they remain attached to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and are bound by its fruits; thus, they are unwilling to purify Buddha-lands or transform sentient beings.
Those who uphold this sutra have only just attained the perfect cause (*hetu*) and are not yet said to have realized the fruit (*phala*).

Since the merit of their causal mind is already equal to that of the Arhat fruit, one can know that the merit of the stage of fruition is inconceivable. Someone might say: "If it is already the cause..."

[The questioner asks: "Regarding the mind: Is there perhaps such a person in the world? [The respondent] says: "Indeed, there are such people. I am ashamed that my own knowledge is shallow and I cannot remember extensively;
