furthermore, I lack the perfect mirror-like wisdom of a sage. For now, I shall briefly cite one or two examples from what I have heard to resolve the doubts of you, the sons of the Śākya.

For instance, when Li Lou sees ants fighting across a mountain, this is the power of the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*). When Cai Wenji hears the sound of a sawing outside a wall, this is the power of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).

The lute strings are the faculty of hearing. Nāgārjuna’s ability to distinguish pills of a hundred flavors is the faculty of smell. Zhuge Liang’s ability to discern the waters of the Fu River is the faculty of taste.
Fotudeng’s manifestation of military formations in his palm is the faculty of touch. Zhang Zai’s distant prognostication of the future is the faculty of mind.
It is said that these [abilities] were not obtained by hearing and upholding the sutras; I have merely spoken of them as they pertain to their respective capacities.

I am ashamed that I lack the holy wisdom of perfect discernment; how could I know whether he did not uphold this sutra in his previous lives? You need only believe the Buddha’s words with earnest faith;
they are certainly not false or erroneous.
— *The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging*
The preceding section clarified that the merit of a single phrase of sympathetic joy (*anumodanā*) surpasses that of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*).

Regarding the purification of the six sense faculties through reading, reciting, receiving, and upholding [the sutra], it is not yet known who has ever attained such a state; therefore, the example of *Sadāparibhūta* (Never-Disparaging) is cited as proof. This is an instance of using a person to verify the Dharma.
There are two aspects to *Sadāparibhūta*: first, there is the one who does not specialize in reading or reciting, but merely upholds a single phrase and exhorts others to attain [it].
Regarding those who attain the purity of the six sense faculties: first, this is a sign of the sudden awakening of one's own mind.

It means that prior to the arising of a single thought, such Buddha-nature is fully possessed by every person; they shall certainly become Buddhas, and thus one must not dare to treat them with contempt.

How is it known to be a sign of the sudden awakening of one's own mind? This chapter begins by discussing the merits and faults of upholding or violating [the precepts], and subsequently states that there is no fault...
For immeasurable, inconceivable, and incalculable (*asaṃkhyeya*) kalpas—does this not clarify that the past of this mind is beginningless and cannot be limited by the calculation of time?
As for the Buddha named King Awesome Sound (*Vaiśvānara-rāja*), does he not say that this mind is the sound of no-sound, its majesty being supreme and its sovereignty like that of a king?
It is like the Way of Heaven: when it brings forth life, it does so universally.

When the world undergoes growth and transformation, and when there is the stern and killing [of winter], then the entire world experiences that stern and killing. It is enacted without being commanded; it is believed without words being spoken.
Since Heaven and Earth have no sound, yet the world receives their majestic commands to harmonize their transformations—is this not indeed sovereign freedom?

The true reality of one’s own mind is likewise so. If one attempts to evaluate it through written characters and spoken language, then throughout past and present, ancient and modern, among the noble and the ordinary, the heterodox and the orthodox, right and wrong, and self and other—such things would be beyond description;

how then could its transformative power be brought to universal realization? Because it is without sound, nothing can escape its majestic command. Yet the principle of true reality is such that there is no word that does not [express it].
Because it is obstructed by words, he likewise employs the teaching of the Three Vehicles.

As for the Buddha’s lifespan of forty quadrillion *nayuta* Ganges-sand eons, this is the principle beyond words; it does not fall into stages or ranks, but transcends the merits of the forty levels far beyond.
That both the True Dharma and the Semblance Dharma are as numerous as the atoms of the world refers to a number that transcends all calculation.
The teaching of King Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja) penetrates both past and present; there is no dharma that is not it. How could it be limited by numerical quantity?
Furthermore, there is another Buddha who appears and is also named King Majestic Sound; this is the second doctrinal gate. Although within the first gate there is no verbal teaching, it is not so.

To prevent confusion, I have provisionally established this teaching at the second gate, using the metaphorical designation of the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) to reveal, cause awakening to, and lead others into [the truth].

Thus, the fact that there were twenty-two thousand million Buddhas all bearing the same name indicates that from the skillful means (*upāya*) of the One Vehicle, the distinctions of the Two Vehicles were opened forth.

Regarding the statement that the first Tathāgata, King of Majestic Sound (*Bhīṣmagarjitasvararāja*), entered parinirvāṇa during the Semblance Dharma (*saddharmapratirūpaka*): the Semblance Dharma is...
This refers to verbal teachings. When verbal teachings arise, the true nature (dharmatā) vanishes; therefore, it is said that the True Dharma is extinguished.
Once the true nature has vanished, sentient beings compete to cling to these verbal teachings. Thus it is said: "Arrogant bhikṣus possess great power.

The Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging takes pity on those who compete to cling to verbal teachings, for they cannot penetrate the fundamental reality that transcends words. He directly points to the true nature within the minds of every person.
They were already fully endowed with Buddhahood from the very beginning. Therefore it was said: "I deeply respect you all; I do not dare to treat you with contempt.
You are all practicing the Bodhisattva path and shall surely attain Buddhahood. Because this was a direct pointing-out, they did not recite the scriptures but practiced only prostrations.
The fourfold assembly, being stubbornly attached to the literal teachings, could not believe this direct pointing-out upon hearing it; instead, they spoke of it with malicious words.
Though he was reviled, struck with staves and stones, and pelted, the Bodhisattva continued to call out to him in a loud voice.
How profound and earnest was his heart of compassion! When the bhikṣu was approaching death, he fully heard the Dharma of the former Buddhas and attained the purity of the six sense faculties.
This realizes the emptiness of persons. Having realized the emptiness of persons, one transcends birth-and-death within the realms of limited duration;

hence, it says "at the end of his life. As for the statement that he further increased his lifespan by two hundred trillion nayutas of years: this refers to his renewed cultivation of the two contemplations to shatter attachment to dharmas.

Once attachment to dharmas is shattered, provisional and ultimate teachings proceed together, and he expounds according to what is appropriate; thus, the fourfold assembly all come to believe and submit. Life...

That he ultimately encounters two thousand *koṭi* Buddhas signifies the realization of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*). Upon attaining the emptiness of phenomena, one transcends the生死 (*saṃsāra*) of transformation;

therefore, it is further stated that his "life comes to an end. Having thoroughly mastered the two kinds of emptiness and skillfully understood the provisional and the real, he is about to approach the three types of wisdom (*trividya*).

Thus, the name of the Buddha he encounters is Candrasūryapradīpa (Sun-Moon-Lamp-Clarity). Such perfect and luminous threefold wisdom does not transcend the two categories of the provisional and the real. Therefore...
There were two thousand billion [beings]. Having drawn near to the three wisdoms (*trijñāna*), they were able to practice both compassion and wisdom together.
Their compassion benefited all beings with the sovereignty of a cloud; their wisdom destroyed delusions like a lamp dispelling darkness. "King" (*rāja*) also carries the meaning of sovereignty;

therefore, the Buddha they encountered was named Cloud Sovereign Lamp King (*Abhrajālin-īśvara-pradīpa-rāja*). He preached the Dharma for the multitude, and those who heard it attained the purity of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi*).
The previous realization of the emptiness of persons is empty by way of being devoid of existence; therefore, it is described simply as "purity.
This realization of the emptiness of phenomena is empty while being existent; therefore, it is called the "eternal eye. Otherwise, there would be the fault of redundancy.

Regarding the phrase "making offerings to such various Buddhas," this refers to the aforementioned Buddhas, all of whom are one's own mind. Thus, Jiyin said: "Making offerings and drawing near [to them]."
This is the meaning of observing in accordance with reality. One should know that King Majestic Sound (Vaiśvānara-rāja) is the meaning of one’s own mind being pure and free from discursive thought;

the Sun-Moon-Lamp Radiance (Sūryacandrapradīpa) is the meaning of the three wisdoms of one’s own mind being perfectly luminous; and the Cloud-Sovereign-Lamp King (Meghasvararāja) is the meaning of compassion and wisdom operating in unison within one’s own mind.
As these qualities gradually dissolve back into oneself, it is said: "The One Who Is Never Disparaging is none other than my own self."
Based on this, it should be known that my statement regarding the sudden realization of one's own mind is not false or exaggerated.

One who can believe that their own mind is the Buddha, though not yet perfected, shall attain it before long. Therefore, it is said: "Because I have upheld, maintained, read, and recited this sutra, I have swiftly attained Bodhi.
Yet those four assemblies cling tenaciously to the literal teachings and do not believe that their own minds [are the Buddha]. Nevertheless, regarding their own minds...
There is no decrease. Therefore, even though one may not encounter the Triple Gem for many kalpas and fall into hell, one still manages to encounter [the Buddha] Not-Disparaging and achieve Bodhi.
Is this not the realization of one's own mind that leads to accomplishment?

Even when subjected to verbal abuse, insults, or struck with sticks and stones, one plants the seeds of enlightenment through such disparagement and abuse—just as a person might despise a sandalwood tree.
With an evil mind he cut down the tree; because of cutting the tree, the fragrance followed his body. Thus one knows that one’s own true mind is without beginning and without end:
it does not increase when in the state of a sage, nor does it decrease when dwelling among ordinary people. It is like empty space—neither can it be sought, nor can it be escaped.
Because the Buddha knew this, he cited an analogy to bring it forth. If one awakens to one's own mind, then one will know that the Buddha originally did not speak to the Buddha.
The Bodhisattvas, numbering as many as the atoms in a thousand worlds, are none other than the sentient beings of the Dharma-realm.

Because they heard the words of Never-Disparaging, "All of you shall become Buddhas," the ten realms simultaneously awakened to the One Mind; thus, they surged forth from the ground of the mind of ignorance.
Having attained awakening himself, he took pity on those who had not yet heard the truth; thus, he made a vow to uphold this sutra.

When it says, "In the lands where the emanations reside and the places where they pass into extinction after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa," these "emanations" refer to the various teachings of the sutras—that is, the Dharma-body manifested through the Tathāgata’s spoken word.
Sentient beings in the final age possess meager virtue and heavy defilements, and false views arise perversely; consequently, the True Dharma...

Because [delusions] have been obliterated, it is called "extinction" (nirvāṇa). The Bodhisattva awakens to the knowledge that the wondrous Dharma of the human mind is inherently possessed by all people;
therefore, he makes a vow to propagate and uphold it, so as to cause them to sever false views and awaken to their own minds. Thus, the Bodhisattvas of a thousand worlds vow to propagate this sutra.

As for the World-Honored One manifesting supernatural powers before the long-resident bodhisattvas of this Sahā world and the fourfold assembly, his intention lies in ensuring that [the Dharma] circulates universally both here and there.
That the mark of his tongue reaches up to the Brahma Heaven signifies vertical penetration through the three periods of time.
That light from his pores illuminates the ten directions signifies horizontal pervasion throughout the ten directions. Thus, he vertically penetrates and horizontally pervades. Not...
It arises from a single mind. Therefore, I entrust this to you, urging you one after another to each uphold and propagate it so that it shall not be severed.
This Dharma is not unique to me alone; the Buddhas of the ten directions likewise emit light and entrust it, and there is none who does not act in this same way.

In the preceding "Chapter on Expedient Means," the Buddhas of the ten directions were cited to collectively bear witness to this mind; here, the Buddhas of the ten directions collectively entrust this mind.

From beginning to end, it forms a single, coherent whole. That a period exceeding a single sitting session fills hundreds of thousands of years is due to the inconceivable power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*).
That the faint sounds of a finger-snap or a cough resonate throughout the ten directions is the manifestation of the subtlest light.
These manifestations all reveal the entire substance of the wondrous Dharma (*dharmadhātu*). When the wondrous Dharma manifests, it necessarily shatters ignorance (*avidyā*);
therefore, the earth quakes in six ways. Sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance; their faculties and capacities are deluded and limited, preventing them from observing universally.
Once ignorance is shattered, one can then illuminate the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) perfectly; thus, they behold the boundless transformation Buddhas, Śākyamuni, and Prabhūtaratna within this land.

When the fourfold assembly of bodhisattvas and others in the gathering had attained awakening, their compassion extended to those in distant regions; thus, the deities in the heavens proclaimed this news.
Upon hearing it, sentient beings each took refuge, invoked the name [of the Buddha], and offered worship. By doing so, they awakened to their own minds and gave rise to sublime practice.
Because of these subtle causes, they will surely attain the fruit of Buddhahood; therefore, the articles of offering were transformed into jeweled canopies that pervaded everywhere.
It covers all Buddhas above. When ignorance is destroyed, self and others are no longer separated; thus, the worlds of the ten directions are unimpeded and pervasive, like a single Buddha-land.
Having awakened to one’s own mind, one’s task is complete and it is now fit to entrust [the teaching].
Therefore, he addresses the Bodhisattva Śūraṅgama and the others. However, this wondrous Dharma is inconceivable; for this reason, I and all the Buddhas, by means of—
Such supernatural powers, even if praised for their merits throughout immeasurable eons, could never be fully exhausted.
To state the essentials, they do not exceed four kinds. All existing phenomena constitute the totality;
all sovereign supernatural powers are *prajñā* (wisdom); all secret and essential treasuries are *vimukti* (liberation); and all most profound matters are [the *dharmakāya*].
The Dharma-body. Such teachings as these are all proclaimed and clearly expounded in this sutra.
Therefore, you should receive and uphold them with a single mind.
(Entrustment Chapter)
Regarding the act of stroking the Bodhisattva’s crown with the right hand: the right is considered correct. Stroking the crown signifies the intent of providing consolation;

it manifests that this Dharma is correct and in accord with liberation. The Dharma of Bodhi, which has been cultivated for immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, is precisely this subtle and wondrous self-mind.
This mind is difficult to believe in and difficult to understand; [the Buddha] desires to cause the great assembly...
All have awakened to this mind. Therefore it is said: "I now entrust this to you. Since the great assembly has awakened, they should also cause it to reach all future sentient beings.
Therefore it is said: "Circulate it with one mind and cause it to increase extensively.

Furthermore, the term *samaya* (threefold samaya) signifies repeated entrustment, manifesting that this Dharma is exhausted without remainder. Regarding the passage beginning "The Tathāgata possesses great compassion," [the word] *maitrī* (compassion) refers to...
It can bestow happiness; compassion can extract suffering. Because it bestows happiness, it can grant sentient beings the Buddha’s wisdom, the Tathāgata’s wisdom, and self-arisen wisdom.
Because it extracts suffering, when sentient beings lack faith, it demonstrates, instructs, benefits, and gladdens them regarding other profound dharmas.
Because it is free from stinginess, it makes no distinction between those who are near or distant, universally desiring that they hear [the teaching]. Because it is without fear, it has no dread.
Māra and the outsiders, I entrust this to you with a loud voice. Such is the mind of the Buddha; you all should likewise look up to and study the Tathāgata.
Do not give rise to stinginess or parsimony. In future ages, expound this sutra extensively for the sake of sentient beings; this shall be your repayment of the Buddha’s grace.
The Bodhisattvas, having deeply realized the Buddha’s mind, likewise received his instructions three times.

Having entrusted the Dharma to worthy recipients, and as the Dharma assembly was about to conclude, he commanded the manifested Buddhas to each return to their respective abodes, and the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna to return to its original state.
The manifested Buddhas represent the Dharma of expedient origination, while the Stūpa of Prabhūtaratna represents the principle of the true mind and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*). Why?
It serves as the condition for dependent origination, meaning that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and arise from conditions.

Just as sentient beings are deluded by their own minds and undergo the cycle of rebirth in vain, the Buddha taught the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths to lead them toward the pursuit of Nirvana. If birth and death are eliminated, Nirvana does not exist as a separate entity;

therefore, it is like a conjured city. The followers of the Two Vehicles dwell within this conjured city, while the Tathāgata provisionally teaches the One Vehicle to guide them back to the [True] Jewel City.
When the conjured city has been left behind, the place of treasure is likewise empty; therefore, it is said to be "near.
For those of great capacity, the Dharma of the Six Perfections is taught directly: generosity is taught because of stinginess and greed; ethical discipline because of the violation of precepts;
patience because of anger and resentment; diligence because of laziness; meditative concentration because of distraction; and wisdom because of ignorance. This is...

This means that [all things] arise from conditions. If stinginess and greed are destroyed, then there is no giving to be practiced. If the violation of precepts is eliminated, then there is no morality to be maintained.
If anger subsides, then there is no patience to be cultivated. If laziness is forgotten, then there is no diligence to be exerted.

If distraction is extinguished, then meditative concentration naturally ceases to exist. If ignorance is emptied, then wisdom does not arise. Therefore it is said: "Each follows its own state of ease."

As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "Luminosity returns to the sun; darkness returns to the dark moon," and so forth. If one realizes that dependent origination is without arising, then the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) is unmoving;

thus it is said that "they may return to their original state. Now, while the manifested bodies each return, yet Many Treasures (*Prabhūtaratna*) remains as he was, this is precisely what the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* means when it says:
"All things that can return are naturally not you; that which does not return to you is not you."
Who? It is that which is called "the shedding of all skin until only the single reality remains. Thus has the Tathāgata entrusted [this teaching], and thus shall the Bodhisattvas uphold it;
we, too, should likewise realize it. If one turns it back and lets it dissolve, then the Many-Jeweled Stūpa (Prabhūtaratna) is my very own body.
When they meet in ease and harmony, the manifested Buddhas are fundamentally not external dharmas. To receive this with a great mind, in a single instant—
One can then achieve liberation. Yet, with even slight doubts, one may fail to return to the source for as many kalpas as there are grains of sand.

In the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja Bodhisattva," the emptiness of both person and phenomena constitutes the original power of the Bodhisattva and the sovereign medicine for sentient beings. Sentient beings, however, cling to these two...

Seeing that the affliction of dogmatic attachment had arisen, the Bodhisattva demonstrated the cultivation of the two types of emptiness to shatter their stubborn clinging; thus he received this name.

As for Śrīgarbha (Sudhana), because he initiated past causal practices through the wisdom of his former lives and maintained them with sovereign mastery, he in turn asked about the fundamental deeds of the Medicine King.
Because these two attachments were heavy and difficult to break, it is said that "there are again immeasurable [others]."
Regarding these difficult practices and ascetic austerities, it is thus that Suvarnapuspa clearly perceives them without error.

It was in order to cause sentient beings to know their fundamental reality that he provisionally raised this question. As for the Buddha named Candrasūryavimalaprabhāsaśrī, because the wisdom realizing the emptiness of persons has not yet exhausted all delusions, his vision is not fully clear, like the moon illuminating the night.
When the wisdom realizing the emptiness of phenomena exhausts all delusions without remainder, vision becomes perfectly clear.
It is clear. Like the sun illuminating the day, the two wisdoms shine perfectly, and the two attachments are simultaneously eliminated; this is called "Pure Bright Virtue.

When the two kinds of emptiness are fully realized, the nature of the three periods of time vanishes; therefore, it was only after immeasurable kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges that this Buddha appeared.
Because the two wisdoms operate in tandem, bodhisattvas and śrāvakas serve as his retinue. Such two wisdoms are perfected instantaneously in a single thought-moment; they are not—
The former is not the latter; thus, it transcends the forty-two stages by far. Therefore, the Buddha’s lifespan is forty-two thousand kalpas.
When the two wisdoms are luminous, one is far removed from defilement; hence, there are no women or evil realms.

Because defilement is abandoned, the resulting environment consists of jeweled grounds and jeweled trees, extending even to banners, canopies, vases, and pedestals—all of which are made of jewels. Indeed, that which is called "Pure Radiance" does not exist apart from the abandonment of defilement.
Purity is purity even while stained; therefore, for the sake of the great assembly, he preaches the Lotus Sūtra.

As for the Bodhisattva named All-Sentient-Beings-Delight-to-See, those of the Two Vehicles seek purity by abandoning defilement; consequently, they are rebuked by the Buddha and despised by the Bodhisattvas.
Sentient beings do not admire his virtue [in its ordinary sense]. The Bodhisattva has heard the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and understands the principle of simultaneous defilement and purity.
He skillfully explains the Dharma according to what is appropriate, conforming to their faculties and providing them with benefit; therefore, he is one whom all sentient beings joyfully behold.

As for the "full twelve thousand years," this refers to cultivating the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), realizing and attesting to the provisional nature of the self, and manifesting births in accordance with the various types of beings; thus, he is able to appear.
In the Sarvarūpakāya-samādhi, one makes offerings by raining down incense and flowers through supernatural power; yet this is not as good as making offerings with the body.
If the grasping at a self has not been extinguished, then there is still the duality of right and wrong. When the self is empty, nothing at all is established.
Therefore, although one may be able to make such offerings, they are not as superior as offering the body itself. The grasping at a self is firm and difficult to shatter; it must...
One cultivates the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination while concurrently practicing the six perfections; thus, the six fragrances symbolize the six pāramitās.

The previous twelve thousand years represent the forward progression (*pravṛtti*) of the twelve links of dependent origination. Since this progression does not obstruct birth, one is able to manifest all form-bodies (*rūpakāya*).
Within this period, reducing ten thousand by one to reach one thousand represents the reversal (*nivṛtti*) of the twelve links of dependent origination. Furthermore, by means of three...
The seventeen chapters serve as its support. Thus, anointing the body with fragrant oil and wrapping it in celestial garments represents being inwardly empowered by the power of patience (*kṣānti*).
Pouring the various fragrant oils represents outwardly relying upon the merits of all Buddhas.

When one thus relies inwardly and relies outwardly, the grasping at a self (*ātman*) is suddenly emptied and true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*) is revealed; therefore, the light shines everywhere throughout eighty billion Ganges Rivers.
In a sand-like world, the Buddhas therein praised him with one voice, saying: "This is true diligence; this is called the true offering of the Dharma.
It surpasses all worldly material offerings. This establishes the meaning that the aforementioned [offerings] are not equal to the offering of one's own body.
That his body was finally exhausted after it had burned for twelve hundred years is due to the wisdom of self-emptiness (*ātma-śūnyatā-jñāna*).
Contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination, one realizes they are utterly ungraspable; only then does the grasping at a self become empty.

When the grasping at a self is empty, one transcends the birth-and-death of the limited realm (paricchinna-saṃsāra); hence it is said that "life has ended. However, because the grasping at phenomena (dharma-grāha) is not yet empty, one has not yet crossed over the birth-and-death of transformation (pariṇāma-śarīra).

Therefore, one is born by transformation back into the original land. This transformative nourishment of birth relies upon pure merit and differs from the limited realm, which relies upon defiled craving. Thus, the father is named...
"Pure Virtue. The Buddha Sun-Moon Pure Brightness-Virtue still exists in the present... even until I now return to make offerings to this Buddha.

This reveals that although the state of fruition is immovable and the nature of the three periods of time is empty, there is coming and going due to causes, and birth and death appear vividly as they are.
This is the purport for the circulation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. The followers of the Two Vehicles cling to the body as having a self;

they believe there is birth-and-death from which one may escape and a nirvana that can be realized. The Bodhisattva burns his own body to demonstrate that such clinging is erroneous. If [the self] were truly existent, [this would not be necessary].

"As I burn this body, who is it that transcends birth and death? Who is it that realizes nirvana? The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) cling to the notion that the body is without self, that upon one death there is annihilation and no further rebirth.
Yet as I burn this body, I shall be reborn through transformation; how could this be annihilation?
In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, King Prasenajit used inference (*anumāna*) to conclude that his own body would certainly perish. The World-Honored One likewise [taught]..."
Inference leads one to realize that the vision of the river is fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing;

yet this does not compare to this Bodhisattva, who directly demonstrates with his own body both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-non-ceasing, making it crystal clear and evident. For this reason, he is the Medicine King for humans and devas.

The son’s white-robed return to the Buddha’s presence is a symbol of the movement from cause toward fruit. The Buddha’s seeing him and immediately proclaiming his parinirvāṇa is a symbol of the cessation of the fruit once the cause has been fulfilled.
It is like seeds of grain or wheat: when the sprout appears, the seed perishes.
This clarifies the meaning that extinction is itself non-extinction. That the Bodhisattva was moved by grief and distress—this "grief" refers to grieving over the extinction of the Eye of the World.

Because one’s resonance connects with the Buddha’s mind through transmission, one gathers the śarīra relics and erects eighty-four thousand stūpas to cause others to look up to them with reverence and repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Even though one performs such offerings, if the mind is still not satisfied, it is because attachment to phenomena (*dharmagrāha*) has not been emptied.
Such offerings are all mundane, conditioned characteristics; they do not compare to the supramundane, unconditioned [Dharma].

Because [the previous] Dharma was insufficient, it is said that it was not yet enough. However, the arms adorned with a hundred blessings are a symbol for the shattering of the attachment to dharmas (*dharmagrāha*).

Since dharmas possess the quality of "guiding and maintaining" (*nīti-dhṛti*), they are like hands capable of grasping and holding. Thus, having previously shattered the attachment to the self (*ātman-grāha*) by relying on the contemplation of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*), he speaks of "twelve hundred years.
Within this, there are two kinds of attachment to dharmas which rely upon the seventh consciousness (*kliṣṭa-manas*); to shatter this attachment, one must empty the seventh.

Regarding the seven consciousnesses, it is therefore said that [the duration] is seventy-two thousand years. Although the six consciousnesses of the two vehicles are empty, the seventh consciousness remains entirely present.

Failing to believe in the existence of the eighth consciousness, they instead cling to this seventh consciousness as being *nirvāṇa*. Once the seventh consciousness is dismantled, the eighth consciousness manifests before them.
One then realizes that this consciousness contains all the seeds of both the mundane and supramundane realms; thus, everyone is capable [of awakening].
Having attained Buddhahood, he caused countless seekers of the Śrāvaka vehicle to resolve upon Bodhicitta and attain the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Forms (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana*).
When Bodhisattvas, humans, devas, and others saw him without arms, they were filled with grief and lamentation.

For Bodhisattvas and devas alike, practicing conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) deeds was their primary duty; now that those conditioned practices have been shattered, it appears as though something is missing.
Because one side was missing, it was said that his body was incomplete. The Bodhisattva thought to himself:

"I renounce the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) to enter the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), for the sake of seeking all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*). Within this all-encompassing wisdom, there is nothing that is not accomplished through the unconditioned.
Therefore he said: "By renouncing both my arms, I shall surely attain the golden-colored body of a Buddha. If this is true and not false, let my two [arms]..."

His arm was restored to its former state, thereby demonstrating that it is only his attachment that is destroyed, not the Dharma itself. When the two attachments are eliminated, ignorance is shattered;
hence the earth shook in all directions. When the two kinds of emptiness are realized, merit is manifested; hence the heavens rained down precious flowers.
However, to burn one's body and arms, to shatter the two attachments, and to realize the two emptinesses—is this not the work of sages and worthies? Do not harbor such thoughts.

You should know that he is the Medicine King (Bhaiṣajyarāja) for you all. Therefore it is said: "The Bodhisattva All-Sentient-Beings-Delight-to-See is none other than the present Bodhisattva Medicine King.
Furthermore, sentient beings of ignorance possess [these qualities] in their entirety; those of the Three Vehicles possess them partially; and the Tathāgata has shattered them entirely. Three.

This is the analysis by way of partial destruction. Those who practice the path in later times, even if they cannot achieve complete destruction as the Tathāgata did, should nonetheless practice partial destruction according to the three vehicles.
For example, if one is unable to burn the body or arms like a Bodhisattva, yet can burn a finger or even a toe, this is superior to making offerings of kingdoms, cities, wives, and children.
People today do not understand this and take it to be a literal fact.
There have been those who burned their arms and set their fingers ablaze; yet, as for one who has shattered ignorance and severed the afflictions (*kleśa*), I have not seen such a person.
If it were not for this slight merit of a single finger, how could one transcend the world with its many jewels, kingdoms, cities, wives, and children?
It is because of the destruction of ignorance that the merit of offering the seven treasures of the great trichiliocosm to all Buddhas and noble sages is attained.
In merit, it does not equal even a single four-line verse from this sutra. This sutra points directly to one's own mind to realize the nature of mind and attain Buddhahood;
it is the king of all sutras. Therefore, it is likened to the ocean as the king of all waters, and Mount Sumeru as the king of all mountains.
Even unto the Buddha, who is the sovereign of all dharmas—sentient beings who hear this sutra shall all obtain benefit.
Thus, it is like a cold person obtaining fire, or a naked person obtaining clothing; even as merchants reaching the sea, hearing this sutra, there is no delusion that is not shattered.
Therefore, it is like the sun or a torch, capable of removing all darkness. Furthermore, regarding the copying and making offerings of this sutra, it is the wisdom of the Buddha.
One cannot measure its merit; by hearing the "Chapter on the Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja," one likewise attains immeasurable merit.
If a woman hears this sutra, she shall immediately attain rebirth in the Western Land and will no longer be afflicted by craving and desire.
Such repeated and profound praises of its merit are intended for its circulation—that is, to manifest its wondrousness and exhort its upholding. As an ancient worthy said:
The hundred rivers and myriad streams find their ultimate limit in the sea; the myriad phenomena of the universe find their ultimate limit in space;
all worthy sages find their ultimate limit in the Buddha; and all dharmas find their ultimate limit in the mind. This mind is the great root of total retention (*dhāraṇī*).
The vast source of the myriad dharmas: the World-Honored One has compared this sutra to the ocean and to the Buddha. I say that this sutra is none other than one's own mind;
by inferring from this analogy, it must certainly not be false.
In the "Chapter on the Bodhisattva Gadgadasvara," the Bodhisattva Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, by virtue of upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, attained the *Sarvarūpasaṃdarśana-samādhi*.

This is the faculty of the body (*kāyendriya*). Although he has realized this through the faculty of the body, he had not yet beheld its actual manifestations. When this bodhisattva attained liberation...

The *Sarvasattvarutakauśalya-dhāraṇī* (Dhāraṇī of Skillfulness in the Languages of All Sentient Beings) is precisely the faculty of the tongue; therefore, this [text] follows it to demonstrate its characteristics.

For the manifestation of the body is necessarily accompanied by the preaching of the Dharma, and the preaching of the Dharma is necessarily accompanied by the manifestation of the body, as they are inseparable.

The appearance of the body is like the solar disc rising in the sky: while the object is one, those who behold it perceive it differently—some see it rising from the sea, some see it rising from a mountain, or...
[The Buddha] is seen on rooftops; or seen on plains; some prefer clarity and purity, while others loathe the heat of the sun.

There are thus immeasurable such variations. How could the sun itself possess such [diversity]? Body and tongue are fundamentally one, yet they appear differently according to the diverse capacities of sentient beings.
Thus it is said that he manifests without fixed location, appearing in the forms of Brahmā Kings, Śakra Devendra, and so forth, to preach this sutra. The Buddha emits great...
Regarding the mark of the human form, the radiance of the *uṣṇīṣa* (crown protuberance) signifies that this mind is the supreme summit-dharma (*anuttara-mūrdha-dharma*).
Furthermore, the emission of light from the white tuft (*ūrṇā-kośa*) between the eyebrows signifies that this mind surges forth from the unconditioned Middle Way (*asaṃskṛta-madhyamā-pratipad*).
As for the light illuminating one hundred and eight trillion Buddha-worlds in the eastern direction: the east is the direction of movement; when a sentient being’s single thought-moment moves, then—

One is possessed of the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*). The Sage, having thoroughly realized that movement is non-movement, transcends these one hundred and eight afflictions and realizes the pure *dharmatā*.
Therefore it is said: there is a world named Pure Light Adornment (*Vimalaprabhā-alaṃkāra*), where the Buddha is named Pure Flower Constellation King Wisdom (*Vimalapuṣpa-jyotiṣprabha-rāja-jñāna*).
This very distancing from the one hundred and eight afflictions constitutes the pure cause of the *dharmatā*. By means of such a cause...
He arouses his wisdom from former lives, for he has attained mastery over all dharmas. Thus he illuminates that land.
When the Bodhisattva Miaoyin (Wonderful Sound) speaks of how [the Buddha] has long planted the roots of virtue and so forth, this refers to the arousal of wisdom from former lives.

Because of the illumination, he addresses that Buddha, desiring to come to this land; this is the introductory prologue. The Buddha then admonishes him not to give rise to inferior thoughts and so forth.
This means that he instructs one to observe with equanimity, secretly revealing that the traces manifested by Śākyamuni are not his actual retribution-body (*vipākakāya*).

As for his use of the power of *samādhi* to transform eighty-four thousand lotus flowers, this signifies the transformation of the eighty-four thousand afflictions (*kleśa*) into the eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates.
Afflictions are defilement; Dharma-gates are purity. It is not that the Dharma exists apart from the afflictions.
The gate: taking afflictions (*kleśa*) themselves as the Dharma-gate, it is therefore called the "Lotus.
When Mañjuśrī beheld this and addressed the Buddha, he was indicating that taking afflictions as the Dharma-gate cannot be known in its full extent except through fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).

When Mañjuśrī inquired about the roots of goodness and merit [of Gadgadasvara], the Buddha told him that it was because Prabhūtaratna manifested his sign that Gadgadasvara appeared with the lotus. This is...

The Dharma-gate of worldly afflictions (*kleśa*) is the principle of non-duality. Since the Dharma-gate of worldly afflictions is governed by the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), only true wisdom (*bhūtajñāna*) can lead one through it.
When Prabhūtaratna addressed Gadgadasvara, he was using the provisional to summon the real.
That Gadgadasvara passed away in that land and came together with eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas signifies entering the Dharma while carrying worldly afflictions.
It is a gateway. To enter the Dharma-gate, one must necessarily shatter ignorance; therefore, the lands of all the countries he passes through tremble.
When ignorance is shattered, merit becomes manifest; therefore, precious lotus flowers rain down and celestial music is played.

The Bodhisattva’s eyes are like the petals of a blue lotus, and his face surpasses hundreds of thousands of millions of moons; even with all such marks fully perfected, he emerges from the toils of worldly existence and realizes [enlightenment].

The true mark (*dharmatā*) is the majestic and solitary manifestation of the Dharma-body and Reward-body (*dharmakāya* and *sambhogakāya*). Having seen the Buddha, he describes his respectful demeanor, further saying:
"I now wish to see the body of the Buddha Prabhūtaratna; I only pray that the World-Honored One will show it to me.

Here, Prabhūtaratna represents ultimate wisdom (*jñāna*), while Śākyamuni represents provisional wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). Miaoyin (Ghoṣadatta) represents provisional practice. Through the skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) of provisional practice, he manifests coming and going. [End of previous section]
Thus, that land hears from afar; this clarifies that while the provisional and the real appear distant, they are not distant. Here, [the assembly] does not see beneath their seats;
this clarifies that while the provisional and the real appear near, they are not near. The previous instance of Prabhūtaratna’s mutual address was using the Real to summon the Provisional.

This instance of Śākyamuni’s manifestation is using the Provisional to guide toward the Real. Prabhūtaratna’s praise signifies the harmonious accord between wisdom and practice. As for the preceding...

Thus, Mañjuśrī makes his request. This "Huade" (Flower Virtue) who asks further questions represents the cause and practice: "Hua" (Flower) symbolizes the causal conduct, while "De" (Virtue) refers to merit.

He inquires about the roots of goodness and meritorious virtues cultivated in past lives in order to respond to Mañjuśrī’s request; therefore, he asks what roots of goodness were planted and what merits were cultivated.
He describes the Buddha upon whom he relies, named King Cloud-Thunder-Sound (*Meghadundubhisvara-rāja*); "Cloud" symbolizes compassion.

Thunder manifests majesty. Possessing both virtues, he preaches the Dharma with sovereign mastery; thus he is called King of Sound. Wondrous sound manifests practice, for practice issues forth from the essence.
Furthermore, wondrous practice must necessarily depend upon a wondrous essence. How is this known? It is like the silence of thunder:
a single roll of it causes a hundred *li* to tremble, yet the people within those hundred *li* each hear it differently. Or...

Upon hearing it, some attained awakening; some, upon hearing it, practiced self-reflection and cultivation; some, upon hearing it, gave rise to joy; and some, upon hearing it, were moved to awe and dread.
With a single wondrous voice, he skillfully adapted to the various capacities of sentient beings.
Is this not because wondrous practice issues forth from the wondrous essence? Since it flows forth from the wondrous essence, it is said: "You see only the body of the Bodhisattva Wondrous Sound."
While remaining here, they do not know that they manifest various bodies everywhere to preach this sutra for the sake of all sentient beings.
When asked about their samādhi, they say it is the "Manifestation of All Physical Bodies" (*sarvarūpasaṃdarśana*).

As for the eighty-four thousand bodhisattvas who have all attained this samādhi, it is what is called "realizing the one is to realize all"; every faculty and every object enters into perfect penetration. Thus it is said.

Regarding the phrase "having completed the Buddha-work, he returns to his original land": this clarifies that these wondrous practices are never separated from one's fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
People today merely see the sages and worthies achieve supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) and samādhis, conceiving thoughts of wonder and rarity;

they do not know that these have come about through the roots of goodness and merit cultivated over vast eons. Because they do not understand this, they are unwilling to practice. For this reason, the World-Honored One—
This wondrous practice is expounded for the purpose of circulation and exhortation.

Prior to the "Universal Gate" chapter of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, Bhaiṣajyarāja represents the faculty of the body, Gadgadasvara represents the faculty of the tongue, and this bodhisattva [Samantabhadra] corresponds to the faculty of the mind. These three—
When sentient beings grasp at dharmas, they give rise to the three obstacles—namely, afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering (*duḥkha*).

When Bodhisattvas attain liberation, these are transformed into the three virtues—namely, compassion (*karuṇā*), wisdom (*prajñā*), and practice (*caryā*). King of Medicine represents wisdom; Wonderful Sound represents practice; and Avalokiteśvara represents compassion.
Although wisdom and practice benefit both self and others, their primary benefit lies in the self. Compassion likewise benefits both self and others, yet its primary benefit lies in [others].

Therefore it is said: "Do not contemplate the sound; contemplate with the contemplator. In the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, the entry into the Way is described solely through the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*).

Here, however, the merits are being formally enumerated, and thus compassion is also included. It is precisely this faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) that fully encompasses the merits of all six faculties;
therefore, one attains the two kinds of supreme excellence of the Tathāgata. The first is: above, it harmonizes with the ten directions of all Buddhas as being of one essence.
The power of compassion. Second, because he unites with the sentient beings of the six realms below, sharing the same aspiration for pity and the same power of compassion;
because the thirty-two manifestations and the nineteen modes of preaching the Dharma share the same aspiration for pity;

and because of the seven calamities, the two requests, and the fourteen fearlessnesses—previously, when [the Buddha] was in the body of Bhaiṣajyarāja, he attained the Samādhi of Manifesting All Physical Bodies, yet its name alone was indicated while its characteristics were not yet shown. Sublime!

The faculty of the ear and the faculty of the tongue, although they manifest their characteristics, merely demonstrate compassionate transformation (*maitrī-vinaya*) and have not yet reached the stage of sympathetic yearning (*karuṇā-utkaṇṭhā*).

Herein, the faculty of the mind (*manas-indriya*) is such that through compassion it preaches the Dharma to bestow happiness, and through pity it seeks out sounds to rescue beings from suffering. In this way, the three faculties of body, speech, and mind all attain the name of "wondrous.

While they differ in degree regarding their hidden functions, they equally propagate the wondrous Dharma. Preaching the Dharma pertains solely to the body and speech; however, as for the extraction of suffering—
The six sense organs respond simultaneously; therefore, it is called the Universal Gate (*Pumen*). What is the Universal Gate?

It is first stated that by merely invoking the name, one contemplates their voices and all attain liberation—is this not a universal response? Furthermore, as for "even if one enters a great fire, the fire cannot burn them":

seeing and cognition belong to fire, and fire belongs to the mind. When the mind conditions external objects, then subject and object form an opposition, and thus one is burned by the object. [Yet] in a single thought-moment...

Looking back within, the mind is empty and the environment is still; therefore, one is not burned by fire. Formerly, when Dharma Master Lingrun was traveling through the mountains with a group, they encountered a wild fire sweeping rapidly toward them.
His companions urged him to flee, but Lingrun walked at his usual pace as if nothing were happening.

He said, "Outside the mind there is no fire; fire is truly from the mind itself. To think that fire can be escaped is to have no way to avoid it. When the fire reached him, it extinguished of its own accord. How could this be otherwise?

Is this not the power of turning the hearing inward? If one who is being swept away by a great flood can find shallow water simply by reciting the name [of the Buddha], it is because hearing belongs to water, and water belongs to craving (*tṛṣṇā*).
If one turns the hearing inward for even a single thought-moment, the object of sound falls away and the mind of craving becomes thin and faint;
hence it is said that "one immediately finds shallow water. Formerly, when Chan Master Shimen Cong was reprimanded by the Prefect, he cast [himself]...
That one floats upon the water without sinking is also due to the power of reverse contemplation (*pratyavekṣā*).

For those who seek gold, silver, and the like, this refers to the practitioner entering the ocean of the mind to seek the treasure of the Dharma. The black wind is the wind of the objects of ignorance;

the *rākṣasa* is the evil mind of affliction (*kleśa*). When the mind clings to sensory objects, it is devoured by the *rākṣasa* of affliction; yet with a single thought of reverse contemplation, [it is liberated].

Then afflictions are naturally empty; thus, one cannot be harmed by them. Formerly, Prime Minister Yu Di asked Chan Master Tongziyu, "What is it like to be blown by black winds and fall into the land of the rākṣasa demons?
The Master said, "Yu Di, you hired laborer! Why do you ask such a thing?
The official suddenly turned red with anger. The Master said, "This very [anger] is what it means to be blown by black winds and fall into the land of the rākṣasas."
The Land of Ghosts: Is it not the case that the rākṣasas are the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the black wind is the external object?

Those on the verge of being harmed are the sense faculties encountering their objects. To call out the name is to turn the gaze inward. When the mind and the object oppose one another, one will inevitably be harmed;
when the mind can turn the gaze inward, the external object vanishes of its own accord. Thus, the sword is immediately shattered into pieces. Formerly, Emperor Taiwu of the Wei dynasty...
Daowen listened to the words of Cui Hao and executed the śramaṇas of the empire. One day, Dharma Master Tanshi stood at the palace gate with his *khakkhara* staff;
the gatekeeper reported this to Daowen, who ordered that he be executed according to military law. Though he was repeatedly beheaded, he remained unhurt.

Daowen was greatly incensed and personally struck him with the sword he wore at his waist, yet it could not wound him. He was also like Sun Jingde, for whom the blade [refused to cut] as he faced execution.
These suppressions are all the result of the power of inward reflection (*pratyavekṣā*). As for the *yakṣas* and *rākṣasas* that fill the three thousand great thousandfold world-systems:
the *rākṣasas* in the sea before one are the afflictions within the practitioner’s own mind;

the *yakṣas* and *rākṣasas* in this central world-system are those with evil minds in the world who wish to come and disturb people—that is, evil persons seeking out opportunities to cause trouble. To invoke [their names]...
This means that one should cultivate goodness as a means of retreat and evasion. If one meets evil with evil, that evil will only blaze more fiercely, leaving no way to escape.
If one cultivates goodness with a single mind, then those evil persons will feel ashamed of themselves and will be unable to cause harm.
Formerly, Lin Xiangru and Lian Po served King Zhao together. Lian Po considered his own merits to be superior and resented Xiangru’s rank being higher than his; every time...
[The Emperor] wished to humiliate him, but Sima Xiangru avoided him each time. Eventually, Bo realized his transgression and apologized with a staff of thorns upon his back.

Is this not a superior strategy for repelling evil through withdrawal and avoidance? The shackles, fetters, and collars that bind one’s body—these shackles, fetters, and collars are none other than the five desires, fame, and profit.
To utter these names is itself liberation and awakening. The people of the world are bound by the five desires, fame, and profit.
It is worse than shackles. If one can awaken in a single thought to their unreality, then the shackles will fall away of their own accord.
Long ago, Tianran was traveling to Chang’an to seek an official post when he encountered a Chan practitioner on the road. The practitioner asked him, “Where does the road to Chang’an lead?

Tianran replied, “To what end do you ask about Chang’an? The practitioner said, “To seek an official post. The practitioner then asked, “How does seeking an official post compare to seeking Buddhahood? Tianran replied, “Seeking...”
"Where is the Buddha going? [The monk] replied, "Have you not heard that the Great Master Ma has opened a field for the selection of Buddhas in Jiangxi?
Having said this, he shook out his sleeves and departed. Jiyin said: "By nature he is like a fragrant elephant king, having cast off his shackles to roam free and easy.
Are fame, profit, and the five desires not indeed fetters? He was like a merchant carrying precious treasures."
"Traveling through dangerous paths" refers to upholding this sutra in an evil age. Because the sutra is a world-transcending rarity, it is called "precious treasure.
Because the world abounds in heterodoxy, arrogance, and lack of faith, it is called a "dangerous path. "A single person proclaims it" refers to the Buddha’s entrustment to propagate the sutra.

One should possess three qualities. Simultaneously uttering these words, each person shall firmly endure insults and propagate the sutra. By invoking the name of liberation, one shall steadfastly maintain forbearance;
thus, those with false pride and the like will be unable to cause opposition. This is as in the case of the Sutra of the Bodhisattva Never-Disparaging, who upheld the scripture.

Though constantly subjected to verbal abuse and physical assault, because he steadfastly maintained patience, the fourfold assembly was transformed by his influence and could not cause him further distress;
this can serve as verification. Thus, liberation from these seven calamities all relies on the power of reverse contemplation (*pratyavekṣā*), entering through self-awakening.

In a single thought-moment it is perfectly encompassed, and its efficacy can be verified in an instant. If one were to explain this according to conventional phenomena, then one would be seeking it from others—a pursuit that has persisted for a thousand ages.
[The previous] one or two [points] seem somewhat remote; it would be better to focus on the contemplation of the mind.
These—the three poisons, the two types of seeking, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the nineteen modes of preaching the Dharma—are all objects that are the constant manifestations of one's own mind.

If one can contemplate and observe them in accordance with this truth, that constitutes the supreme among all offerings. For this reason, one should uphold the names of the bodhisattvas numbering sixty-two billion *gaṅgā*-sands.

Furthermore, if one were to provide offerings for as long as one lives through four matters, and compare it to receiving and upholding the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva—even for a single moment of prostration and offering—they would be exactly equal and no different.
If one does not reflect back upon one's own mind, then the Bodhisattva would become subject to distinctions of superiority and inferiority.
As for the reason why this Bodhisattva is named Akṣayamati (Inexhaustible Intention), it is because this Bodhisattva, by means of the immeasurable...
One asaṃkhyeya kalpa constitutes a single day. After passing through such immeasurable asaṃkhyeya kalpas, one encounters a single Buddha;
continuing in this manner until one has made offerings to such immeasurable asaṃkhyeya Buddhas, his resolve remains inexhaustible. It is for this reason that he receives this name.
The mind of compassion exists within every person at every moment. If one does not cultivate it with such inexhaustible intent, how could it ever be perfected?

As for the offering of the many precious pearl necklaces from around his own neck to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, it was because he had heard the Buddha praise the supreme excellence of the merit of compassion; thus, throughout such kalpas, he made such offerings.
The wisdom and practices accumulated by the Buddha are all dedicated toward compassion. Wisdom can destroy ignorance, just as a jewel can dispel darkness;

practice can form a continuous connection, just as jewels are strung together to form a necklace. As for Avalokiteśvara’s refusal to accept [offerings], it is because within the realm of perfect penetration there is nothing to be received.
Yet, this state of non-reception does not hinder reception; therefore, the Buddha exhorted him to accept them. Having accepted them, he followed along.

I pay homage to the Two World-Honored Ones. Because they are established based on compassion as the foundation and the two wisdoms of means and reality, they are thus inexhaustible in intention (*akṣayamati*) and the Observer of the World’s Sounds (*Avalokiteśvara*).
In terms of persons, they are the elder and younger brothers; in terms of the Dharma, they are compassion and wisdom.
Neither exists apart from one's own mind. Students should understand this essential meaning.

The *dhāraṇī* chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states that the wondrous Dharma is precisely the subtle and wondrous mind of sentient beings. This mind is free from names and signs; it leaves no trace.
It cannot be expressed by words, nor can it be distinguished through discourse. Therefore it is said: "This Dharma cannot be shown; its verbal expressions are quiescent. Furthermore:
It is said: "This Dharma is of the nature of quiescence and cannot be proclaimed in words. It is further said: "This Dharma cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination.
And it is also said: "This Dharma is exceedingly profound and abstruse; few are able to believe in it. Therefore, it is likened to a bright jewel on the crown of the head:
were one to give it to others, they would all be struck with wonder and alarm; or like the precious treasures in a storehouse: were one to entrust them to others, they would fall to the ground.
They cry out in grievance. Physicians treat them, yet they are instead called incompetent; they do not report [the illness] lightly, considering it to be a delusion.

Thus, being difficult to believe, they frequently encounter resentment and slander. Therefore, the Buddha fully described the benefits of upholding and reciting [this sutra], as well as the faults of slandering and defaming it, earnestly exhorting and admonishing those who propagate the scripture.
They must possess three qualities. Bodhisattva Bhaiṣajyarāja and others deeply understood the Buddha’s intention; therefore—
He spoke of protective dhāraṇīs to ensure that those who uphold this sutra in the末法 (final age) remain far removed from demonic obstacles.
These spoken dhāraṇīs were either taught by sixty-two billion Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, or by forty-two billion Buddhas;

they are the imperial mandates of the Buddhas, transmitted one to another for the purpose of protection and upholding. However, the difficulty of propagating the sutra has existed since ancient times.

It is even so. How could it be otherwise, not only for future generations? If they were not protected by worthy sages and celestial deities, how could those who uphold this sutra during the final five hundred years hope to be free from difficulties? It would be impossible.
The Chapter on the Past Deeds of King Wondrous Adornment (*Su-vyūha-rāja-pūrva-yoga-parivarta*).

Regarding "Wondrous Adornment" (*su-vyūha*): in terms of the Dharma, it refers to adorning one's own mind with loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*). In terms of its traces (*liṅga*), it refers to...

This is to extol and praise the merit of making offerings. As stated repeatedly in the preceding text, when one sees someone who upholds, reads, and recites the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, one should perform various kinds of offerings.
One might think, "The upholder of the sutra is over there; what concern is it of mine? Why should I offer worship?
Therefore, this past event is cited as proof to clarify that the benefit of making offerings is that one shall attain Buddhahood, just like him.
The merit of upholding this sutra is equal and without distinction. In the past, there were four men who formed a fellowship to practice the Way.

While staying in a marketplace, they grew weary of the clamor and bustle, so they moved into the deep mountains. However, as they went back and forth to beg for food, they found it increasingly laborious and exhausting, and were unable to practice the Way.
One person resolved, saying, "While you all practice the Way, I shall go begging for food to provide for you. Because of this, the three people attained the Way.
That one person went in and out of the palace and the marketplace, and upon seeing the king’s noble status, he conceived a heart of longing and was reborn as a king.
The three people deliberated, saying, "He has transmigrated through the worlds for our sake; because of him, we have attained liberation in this body."
"Delivered! We shall go to repay their kindness. One person manifested as a wife, and two persons manifested as sons, so as to deliver them and enable them to attain the Way.
The wife named *Viśuddhaguṇā* (Pure Virtue) signifies "Joy"; as the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa-sūtra* states: "The Dharma-joy is the wife of the Bodhisattva.
The eldest son named *Viśuddhanidhi* (Pure Treasury) signifies "Compassion"; for compassion can bestow happiness, just as a treasury contains jewels, and because it provides abundant benefit. Next...

The name of the son, "Pure Eye" (*Vimalanetra*), signifies compassion (*karuṇā*). Worldly people are blind and lack the eye of wisdom; they constantly fall into the moats and pits of birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

Compassion can extract them from suffering, just as eyes can guide one so that one does not fall into pits or over precipices. "King of Sublime Adornment" (*Sudarśana-rāja*) signifies relinquishment (*tyāga*).
By abandoning false views and practicing the True Dharma, one adorns one's own mind and attains mastery. This is the basis upon which...
The Buddha is named Cloud-Thunder-Sound-Constellation-King-Flower-Wisdom (Meghadundubhisvararājasaṃkusumitābhijña). "Cloud" signifies the meaning of compassionate protection;
"thunder-sound" signifies the meaning of compassionate awakening; and "constellation-king" is the name for a star. The myriad practices are distributed like the arrangement of stars.
"Flower" symbolizes the cause—taking wisdom as the cause—and refers to practicing the myriad deeds of compassion to attain the Bodhi of Buddhahood. This Buddha, moreover...
That which is formed by the union of compassion, wisdom, and practice means that the cause encompasses the ocean of fruition, and the fruition reaches back to the source of the cause.
Furthermore, through compassion, one awakens the causal wisdom of past lives; being sovereign like a king, the character "su" (宿) may also be pronounced with an entering tone (*shù*).
Such causal wisdom is a supramundane dharma, not comparable to worldly dharmas in terms of calculation or measure.

Therefore it is said: In ages long past, beyond immeasurable, boundless, and inconceivable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, there were two sons who possessed great supernormal powers and had long cultivated the path practiced by Bodhisattvas; they appeared in the world with great kindness and great compassion.

Without planting causes over vast eons, one could not achieve such perfection. Because causes were planted over vast eons, she was able to fulfill the six *pāramitās*, as well as the various *samādhis* of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment.

Her desire to go to the Buddha’s dwelling and first inform her mother was what is called the awakening of past causes. As for Pure Virtue (*Viśuddhaguṇā*), she found joy in the Dharma within the Wondrous Adornment (*Vicitravyūha*).
The son represents compassion; the mother embodies the meaning of *Kun* (Earth), which is tranquil and motionless, symbolizing true compassion (*bhūta-karuṇā*).

The son embodies the meanings of *Zhen* (Thunder) and *Gen* (Mountain), capable of generating and uplifting, symbolizing skillful means compassion (*upāya-karuṇā*). The father embodies the meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore it is said:
"Your father believes in and accepts heterodox paths, being deeply attached to the Brahmanical dharma. Skillful means compassion flows forth based upon true wisdom; therefore it is said:
"We are the sons of the Dharma King. Out of skillful means (*upāya*), we guide [beings] by manifesting birth in a defiled age;

therefore, it is said that we are born into families of wrong views. The mother then said to them: "You should take concern for your father and cause him to manifest spiritual transformations," thereby exhorting them to use skillful means to guide and lead him.
Sentient beings are shrouded by ignorance and wander through birth and death; when they are uplifted and received through skillful means, they follow [the path].
This was his transformation. Therefore it is said: "If one should behold him, the mind will surely become pure.

His body surging into the void to a height of seven *tāla* trees and manifesting various supernatural transformations is the sign of employing skillful means to guide and receive [beings]. That the father, seeing this, rejoiced and desired to go to the Buddha’s dwelling is the sign of ignorance following after the transformation.
That the two sons addressed their mother, both wishing to leave the household life, is—namely— [The provided text ends abruptly.]
This is to depart from the house of ignorance. When ignorance is transformed into right view, then the eighty-four thousand afflictions all enter into the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
Therefore, the eighty-four thousand women in the inner palace were all capable of receiving and upholding the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
When ignorance and the afflictions together eliminate false views, the eye of wisdom becomes perfectly clear and one realizes the true mark. One’s own mind...
It is inherently possessed; it is not something newly accomplished for the first time now. Therefore, the Bodhisattva Pure Eye has long since attained mastery of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.

By realizing the true aspect (*dharmatā*), the notions of self and other do not arise. Thus, the Bodhisattva Pure Treasury has, throughout immeasurable eons, attained mastery of the *Samādhi of Departing from All Evil Realms*.
Having realized the true aspect, evil realms are abandoned; thus, he is capable of gathering the teachings of all Buddhas and entering the secret [Dharma].
The secret treasury is thus hidden. In this way, a single mind is fully endowed with all virtues; this is why it is called "wondrous adornment.
As for the two sons using the power of skillful means (*upāya*) to skillfully transform their father—I know this to be the compassion of skillful means.

When the King and the two sons, together with their retinues, go to see the Buddha, ignorance is shattered and the true cause (*tathatā-hetu*) is revealed. When the true cause is revealed, one arrives at...

The Buddha Vehicle is the symbol of progressing from cause toward fruition. The Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma to instruct, benefit, and gladden others is the symbol of realizing the cause through the fruition.
The King’s removal of his pearl necklace to scatter over the Buddha is the symbol of turning the cause toward the fruition.
The manifestation in mid-air of a four-pillared jeweled terrace is the symbol of attaining nirvana by relying upon the Middle Way of the True Mark.

The four legs represent the four virtues. Because one has abandoned the attachments of non-Buddhist false views and is capable of proceeding toward the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*), there is the jeweled throne.
Because one has abandoned the arrogance of the Brahmins and attained the garment of patience (*kṣānti-vastra*), there is the celestial robe.

When the four virtues are complete and false pride is abandoned, one achieves the fruition of the Reward Body (*saṃbhoga-kāya*); therefore, the Buddha sits in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*). This is the praise of the Buddha’s sublime adornments.
One who thoroughly awakens to the fact that the Buddha-fruit is inherently present within one's own mind will easily achieve accomplishment, transcending all conditioned phenomena;
therefore, it is called "the foremost rarity. For one who becomes a bhikṣu within my Dharma, this means abandoning the mundane to pursue the ultimate truth.
As for the Buddha named Śālarāja: because this tree rises higher than all other trees, it is called a "king," symbolizing the attainment of Buddhahood through wondrous adornment and transcendence.

He transcends the three vehicles of humans, devas, and the [other] three vehicles. When the Wheel-Turning King leaves the household life, the Buddha-dharma increases in brilliance; therefore, the country is named "Great Radiance" (*Mahāprabha*).
Because the primary and secondary marks are perfected, the eon is named "Great High King" (*Mahāuccaya-rāja*). Regarding those who practice the Way for eighty-four thousand years:
previously, they entered correct wisdom while still bearing the eighty-four thousand afflictions; here, however, they do so by means of those very eighty-four thousand afflictions.
This constitutes the gate of practice; therefore, it is said that one "practices the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. Because he has profoundly realized the benefit of skillful means (*upāya*), he says:
"These two sons are my spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*); they have come to be born in my household for the sake of benefiting me. This is what the Buddha confirms and approves.

This verifies that the merit of making offerings and upholding this sutra is not in vain. Therefore it is said: "They are able to perform the Buddha's work, instructing, teaching, benefiting, and gladdening others, leading them to enter Bodhi.
The repeated account of the two sons' profound causes is an exhortation to plant roots of goodness.

As for Miaozhuangyan’s praise of the Buddha and his own renunciation of errors and faults, it signifies that once faith is established, it is eternal faith, never again subject to regression. The Buddha told Miaozhuangyan:
The one named Ugra is none other than the Bodhisattva Śrīkūṭa. By means of the flowers of the causes of the ten thousand practices, he adorns the meaning of the four virtues of *nirvāṇa*.
All sentient beings possess eighty-four thousand maladies of defilement (*kleśa*); were it not for the compassion of skillful means, none could provide salvation.
Therefore, at that time, Viśuddhamati and Viśuddhacakṣus—none other than the present-day Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata—having already realized the method...

It then becomes medicine; thus one knows that true compassion is the manifestation of the naturally adorned state of the Dharmadhātu, perfectly illuminated by the light of primordial wisdom (*ādi-bodhi-jñāna*), which is not attained through cultivation.
Therefore, it is represented by the mother. Furthermore, King Susīma’s conversion from the heterodox to the orthodox is like subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭha-labdha-jñāna*);
the lady’s self-awakening within the deep palace, without relying on a teacher, is like fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*). At that time—

One should know that the Sage established his teachings so that both phenomena and principle are fully provided. Without phenomena, one cannot manifest the principle; without principle, one cannot perfect the phenomena.
When phenomena and principle support one another, and both self and others are simultaneously awakened, only then does it accord with the intent of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
In the "Chapter on Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s Exhortation," the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra designates Samantabhadra as the eldest son and Mañjuśrī as the youngest.

In the past, the Bodhisattva Universal Eye sought to see Samantabhadra three times; he entered into samādhi, yet in the end was unable to see him. The Buddha then commanded him to maintain a mental visualization.
Upon paying homage, one sees Samantabhadra Bodhisattva sitting near the Buddha; thus, it is clear that Samantabhadra does not depart from the Buddha's side.
Why, then, is it said here that he comes from the East? It is because the East is the direction of Zhen (the Thunder trigram).

They are all proficient and capable of upholding and maintaining [the Dharma]. What is Samantabhadra? It is precisely the thought of contemplation and application within every person.

It is said: Because awakening is perfectly luminous, the mind is revealed as pure. Because the mind is pure, the objects of perception are pure.

One should know that such a person practices the conduct of Samantabhadra. Therefore, I say that it is precisely within the mind of conceptual thought that [the truth] resides.

When the previous "gate of understanding" was opened, neither contemplation could enter nor could discrimination provide liberation; hence it was said, "It cannot be understood through deliberation or discrimination.
Now that the "gate of practice" is opened, every instance of conceptual thought, contemplation, discrimination, and calculation is, in each case, called "universal" (samanta).
Worthy one, it is thus: the Elephant King with six tusks will appear before that person and speak to them.

The elephant symbolizes the practice of the true nature (dharmatā); the six tusks symbolize the six *pāramitās*. Within the true nature, a single moment of reflection is itself the possession of the six perfections;
this "thinking that is non-thinking" is the meaning of the wondrous Dharma. It is like the Wheel-Turning King hearing the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* from a rishi.

"If it is as you say, then one relies solely on the contemplation of principle and does not rely on the cultivation of phenomena. Since ancient times, has there ever been anyone who actually beheld Samantabhadra?"
It is said that when the wise perform the rite of repentance for twenty-one days, they see the assembly on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa as if it were still present.

To be able to have faith in the thought of one's own mind is the practice of Samantabhadra, and by this, one immediately receives the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s supernatural power. Thus it is.

To understand through faith and resolve, such that there is neither recollection nor non-recollection, is to uphold this sutra. To uphold the sutra in this manner is to hear it directly from the Buddha’s own mouth.

Deeply in accord with the Buddha’s mind, they were thus praised by the Buddha, who stroked their heads and covered them with his robe. Those who understand the true nature of reality (lakṣaṇa) know that the world is like an illusion, and therefore do not crave worldly pleasures.
Skillfully understanding that words and texts are like magical transformations, they do not take pleasure in the scriptures of non-Buddhists.
Nor does he take pleasure in associating with such people. Realizing that the body is like a shadow, he does not become intimate with wicked persons or various forms of female beauty.
Having attained right knowledge and vision, his mind and intentions are upright and honest. Possessing the power of merit and virtue, he is not afflicted by the three poisons and the like.
With no external longings in the mind, one has few desires and is content; thus, one is able to cultivate such practices of Samantabhadra.

Before long, one shall proceed to the site of enlightenment and achieve Bodhi. Furthermore, it clarifies that those who uphold this sutra obtain blessings in the present life, while those who disparage it incur transgressions in the present life.
